nodes.name: First-Order Signature
nodes.question: State the definition: First-Order Signature.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{first-order signature} is a tuple
\[
 \Sigma=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{R},\operatorname{ar}),
\]
where $\mathcal{C}$ is a set of constant symbols, $\mathcal{F}$ is a set of
function symbols, $\mathcal{R}$ is a set of relation symbols, and
\[
 \operatorname{ar}:\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{R}\to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}
\]
assigns to each function or relation symbol its number of arguments.

function symbols, $\mathcal{R}$ is a set of relation symbols, and
\[

\]
assigns to each function or relation symbol its number of arguments.
nodes.formal:

$\operatorname{ar}(s)$ is a positive integer. If $s\in\mathcal{F}$, then
$s$ forms terms with $\operatorname{ar}(s)$ inputs; if $s\in\mathcal{R}$,
then $s$ forms atomic formulas with $\operatorname{ar}(s)$ inputs.

A signature is the formal vocabulary available before any axioms are chosen.
It says which symbols may occur and how many input places each symbol has.

nodes.name: Arity
nodes.question: State the definition: Arity.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\Sigma=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{R},\operatorname{ar})$ be a
first-order signature. The \emph{arity function} is the map
\[
 \operatorname{ar}:\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
\]
that assigns to each function or relation symbol the number of arguments it
requires. When constants are treated as $0$-ary function symbols, the codomain
is enlarged to include $0$.

nodes.name: Language
nodes.question: State the definition: Language.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{first-order language} has two standard readings. As vocabulary, it is
the same data as a signature,
\[
 \mathcal{L}=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{R},\operatorname{ar}).
\]
As a formal language generated by a signature $\Sigma$, it is the set of
well-formed strings built from the alphabet
\[
 A=\Sigma\cup V\cup\Lambda,
\]
where $V$ is a countable set of variables and $\Lambda$ is the fixed stock of
logical symbols and punctuation. In this second reading,
\[
 \mathcal{L}(\Sigma)
 =\{s\in A^* \mid s\in\operatorname{Terms}(\Sigma)
 \text{ or } s\in\operatorname{WFF}(\Sigma)\}.
\]

generated-language reading then selects from all finite strings over $A$ only
the terms and well-formed formulas admitted by the formation rules determined
by $\Sigma$.

nodes.name: Constant Symbol
nodes.question: State the definition: Constant Symbol.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{constant symbol} is a non-logical symbol that behaves syntactically as
a $0$-ary function symbol. In the streamlined convention where constants are
included among function symbols, this is the condition
\[
 \operatorname{Constant}(c)
 \iff c\in\mathcal{F}\text{ and }\operatorname{ar}(c)=0.
\]
Because its arity is $0$, the symbol $c$ is already a well-formed term and
takes no input terms.

nodes.name: Function Symbol
nodes.question: State the definition: Function Symbol.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{function symbol} is a non-logical symbol $f\in\mathcal{F}$ whose
assigned arity determines how many terms it must take as inputs. If
$\operatorname{ar}(f)=n$, then $f$ is an $n$-ary term constructor: it takes
exactly $n$ terms and produces a new term, not a truth value.
nodes.statement_tex:

exactly $n$ terms and produces a new term, not a truth value.

closed on the domain:
\[
  \mathcal{I}(f):M^n\to M.
\]

nodes.name: Relation Symbol
nodes.question: State the definition: Relation Symbol.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{relation symbol}, or predicate symbol, is a non-logical symbol
$R\in\mathcal{R}$ whose assigned arity determines how many terms it must take
as inputs. If $\operatorname{ar}(R)=n$, then $R$ is an $n$-ary formula
constructor: it takes exactly $n$ terms and produces an atomic formula, hence
something with a truth value rather than an object.
nodes.statement_tex:

$R\in\mathcal{R}$ whose assigned arity determines how many terms it must take
as inputs. If $\operatorname{ar}(R)=n$, then $R$ is an $n$-ary formula
constructor: it takes exactly $n$ terms and produces an atomic formula, hence
something with a truth value rather than an object.
nodes.formal:
For every $R\in\mathcal{R}$, if $\operatorname{ar}(R)=n$, then
\[
  R(t_1,\ldots,t_k)\in\operatorname{WFF}(\mathcal{L})
  \iff k=n
\]
whenever $t_1,\ldots,t_k$ are terms. In a structure
$\mathfrak{M}=(M,\mathcal{I})$, the interpretation of $R$ is a subset of
$n$-tuples from the domain:
\[
  \mathcal{I}(R)\subseteq M^n.
\]
Thus $R(t_1,\ldots,t_n)$ is true exactly when the tuple of interpreted terms
lies in $\mathcal{I}(R)$.

$<$ denotes the set of ordered pairs $(a,b)$ such that $a$ is less than $b$.

nodes.name: Axiom
nodes.question: State the definition: Axiom.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a first-order language, and let
$\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$ denote the set of sentences of
$\mathcal{L}$. If $T\subseteq \operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$ is a theory,
then an \emph{axiom of $T$} is an element $\alpha\in T$.

nodes.statement_display:

language.

nodes.source_text:
An axiom system records the assertions chosen for a mathematical setting. Two
axiom systems may use the same language while adopting different assertions.
The shared language fixes the vocabulary; the axiom system fixes the adopted
formal claims.

nodes.name: Theory
nodes.question: State the definition: Theory.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{theory} over a first-order language $\mathcal{L}$ is a collection of
closed sentences in that language:
\[
 T\subseteq\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L}).
\]
If $\Gamma$ is a chosen set of axioms, the theory generated by $\Gamma$ is the
deductive closure
\[
 T=\{\varphi\in\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L})\mid
 \Gamma\vdash\varphi\}.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
A \emph{theory} over a first-order language $\mathcal{L}$ is a collection of
closed sentences in that language:
\[
 T\subseteq\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L}).
\]
If $\Gamma$ is a chosen set of axioms, the theory generated by $\Gamma$ is the
deductive closure
\[
 T=\{\varphi\in\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L})\mid
 \Gamma\vdash\varphi\}.
\]
nodes.formal:
Syntactically, a sentence $\varphi$ belongs to the theory generated by
$\Gamma$ exactly when $\varphi$ is derivable from $\Gamma$. Semantically, for
an $\mathcal{L}$-structure $\mathfrak{M}$, the complete theory of
$\mathfrak{M}$ is
\[
  \operatorname{Th}(\mathfrak{M})
  =\{\varphi\in\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L})\mid
      \mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi\}.
\]
For every sentence $\varphi$, either $\mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi$ or
$\mathfrak{M}\vDash\neg\varphi$, so $\operatorname{Th}(\mathfrak{M})$
decides every sentence of the language.
nodes.fully_quantified_form:

decides every sentence of the language.
nodes.source_text:
A theory is not merely the list of axioms. It is the closure of those axioms
under derivability: every statement that follows from the axioms belongs to
the theory. The axioms start the system; the theory records everything the
system proves.

nodes.name: Theorem
nodes.question: State the definition: Theorem.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{theorem} of a theory $T$ is a sentence $\varphi$ for which there is a
finite formal derivation from $T$, written
\[
 T\vdash\varphi.
\]
Equivalently, in proof-theoretic terms, $\varphi$ is a theorem of $T$ exactly
when some derivation has leaves drawn from logical axioms or sentences of
$T$, uses valid inference rules, and has $\varphi$ as its root.
nodes.statement_tex:
A \emph{theorem} of a theory $T$ is a sentence $\varphi$ for which there is a
finite formal derivation from $T$, written
\[
 T\vdash\varphi.
\]
Equivalently, in proof-theoretic terms, $\varphi$ is a theorem of $T$ exactly
when some derivation has leaves drawn from logical axioms or sentences of
$T$, uses valid inference rules, and has $\varphi$ as its root.
nodes.formal:
Syntactically,
\[
  \operatorname{Theorem}(T,\varphi)
  \iff \exists d\ (d:T\vdash\varphi).
\]
Semantically, $\varphi$ is entailed by $T$ when it is true in every model of
$T$:
\[
  T\vDash\varphi
  \iff
  \forall\mathfrak{M}\,
  \bigl(\mathfrak{M}\vDash T \implies \mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi\bigr).
\]
For first-order logic, the completeness theorem connects these readings:
$T\vdash\varphi$ exactly when $T\vDash\varphi$.

nodes.name: Consequence
nodes.question: State the definition: Consequence.
nodes.statement_display:
A sentence $\varphi$ is a \emph{semantic consequence} of a set of premises
$\Gamma$, written $\Gamma\vDash\varphi$, if every model of $\Gamma$ is also a
model of $\varphi$. Equivalently, there is no structure in which all sentences
of $\Gamma$ are true while $\varphi$ is false.
nodes.statement_tex:

$\Gamma$, written $\Gamma\vDash\varphi$, if every model of $\Gamma$ is also a
model of $\varphi$. Equivalently, there is no structure in which all sentences
of $\Gamma$ are true while $\varphi$ is false.
nodes.formal:
Semantic consequence is the universal condition
\[
  \Gamma\vDash\varphi
  \iff
  \forall\mathfrak{M}\,
  \Bigl(
    (\forall\gamma\in\Gamma,\ \mathfrak{M}\vDash\gamma)
    \implies
    \mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi
  \Bigr).
\]
Syntactic consequence, written $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$, means that there exists
a finite valid deduction of $\varphi$ from $\Gamma$. For first-order logic,
the completeness theorem says that $\Gamma\vDash\varphi$ exactly when
$\Gamma\vdash\varphi$.

nodes.statement_display:

premises. The \emph{deductive closure} of $\Gamma$, denoted
$\operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma)$, is the set of all sentences derivable from
$\Gamma$:
\[
 \operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma)
 =
 \{\varphi\in\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L})\mid
 \Gamma\vdash\varphi\}.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:

nodes.formal:
A set of sentences $T$ is deductively closed exactly when
\[
  T=\operatorname{Cn}(T),
\]
or equivalently, for every sentence $\varphi$,
\[
  T\vdash\varphi \implies \varphi\in T.
\]
The closure operator satisfies the standard Tarskian closure laws:
\[
  \Gamma\subseteq\operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma),
  \qquad
  \Gamma\subseteq\Delta\implies
  \operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma)\subseteq\operatorname{Cn}(\Delta),
  \qquad
  \operatorname{Cn}(\operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma))
  =\operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma).
\]
By completeness for first-order logic, this syntactic closure agrees with the
semantic closure
\[
  \{\varphi\in\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L})\mid
    \Gamma\vDash\varphi\}.
\]

nodes.name: Satisfaction
nodes.question: State the definition: Satisfaction.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\mathfrak{M}=(M,\mathcal{I})$ be an $\mathcal{L}$-structure. A
\emph{variable assignment} is a function $s:\operatorname{Var}\to M$. The
assignment extends recursively to a term-evaluation map $\bar{s}$ by
\[
 \bar{s}(x)=s(x),\qquad
 \bar{s}(c)=\mathcal{I}(c),
\]
and
\[
 \bar{s}\bigl(f(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\bigr)
 =
 \mathcal{I}(f)\bigl(\bar{s}(t_1),\ldots,\bar{s}(t_n)\bigr).
\]
The satisfaction relation $\mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi[s]$ is then defined by
induction on formulas: atomic relations are tested inside the interpreted
relation, equality is interpreted as equality in $M$, Boolean connectives are
interpreted by the corresponding truth operations, and quantifiers range over
all elements of $M$.

all elements of $M$.

nodes.name: Countermodel
nodes.question: State the definition: Countermodel.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\Gamma\subseteq\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$ be a set of premises,
let $\varphi\in\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$, and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be
an $\mathcal{L}$-structure. A \emph{countermodel to the entailment
$\Gamma\vDash\varphi$} is a structure $\mathfrak{M}$ that satisfies every
sentence in $\Gamma$ but does not satisfy $\varphi$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $\Gamma\subseteq\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$ be a set of premises,
let $\varphi\in\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$, and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be
an $\mathcal{L}$-structure. A \emph{countermodel to the entailment
$\Gamma\vDash\varphi$} is a structure $\mathfrak{M}$ that satisfies every
sentence in $\Gamma$ but does not satisfy $\varphi$.
nodes.formal:
For $\Gamma\subseteq\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$ and
$\varphi\in\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$,
\[
  \operatorname{CounterModel}(\mathfrak{M},\Gamma,\varphi)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \bigl(\forall \gamma\in\Gamma,\; \mathfrak{M}\vDash\gamma\bigr)
  \land
  \bigl(\mathfrak{M}\not\vDash\varphi\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, for classical closed sentences,
\[
  \operatorname{CounterModel}(\mathfrak{M},\Gamma,\varphi)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \bigl(\forall \gamma\in\Gamma,\; \mathfrak{M}\vDash\gamma\bigr)
  \land
  \bigl(\mathfrak{M}\vDash\neg\varphi\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:

$\varphi\in\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$,
\[
  \operatorname{CounterModel}(\mathfrak{M},\Gamma,\varphi)

  \bigl(\forall \gamma\in\Gamma,\; \mathfrak{M}\vDash\gamma\bigr)
  \land
  \bigl(\mathfrak{M}\not\vDash\varphi\bigr).
\]

\]

nodes.name: Relative Consistency
nodes.question: State the definition: Relative Consistency.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $T_0$ and $T_1$ be theories. The theory $T_1$ is
\emph{consistent relative to $T_0$} if
\[
 \operatorname{Con}(T_0)\implies \operatorname{Con}(T_1).
\]
Equivalently, every contradiction in $T_1$ would imply a contradiction in
$T_0$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $T_0$ and $T_1$ be theories. The theory $T_1$ is
\emph{consistent relative to $T_0$} if
\[
 \operatorname{Con}(T_0)\implies \operatorname{Con}(T_1).
\]
Equivalently, every contradiction in $T_1$ would imply a contradiction in
$T_0$.
nodes.formal:
For theories $T_0$ and $T_1$,
\[
  \operatorname{RelCon}(T_1,T_0)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \bigl(\neg\exists d_0\,(d_0:T_0\vdash\bot)\bigr)
  \implies
  \bigl(\neg\exists d_1\,(d_1:T_1\vdash\bot)\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, in contrapositive form,
\[
  \exists d_1\,(d_1:T_1\vdash\bot)
  \implies
  \exists d_0\,(d_0:T_0\vdash\bot).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:

\[

\]
Equivalently, in contrapositive form,
\[
  \exists d_1\,(d_1:T_1\vdash\bot)
  \implies
  \exists d_0\,(d_0:T_0\vdash\bot).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Relative consistency does not establish consistency from nothing. It says that
the target theory introduces no new contradiction unless the base theory was
already inconsistent. In practice, a relative consistency proof often gives a
translation that turns any contradiction derived in $T_1$ into a contradiction
derived in $T_0$.

$\{a, b\} \subseteq L$ has both a supremum and an infimum in $L$.

The infimum $\inf\{a,b\}$ is called the \emph{meet} of $a$ and $b$,
written $a \wedge b$.

nodes.name: Complement and Boolean Lattice
nodes.question: State the definition: Complement and Boolean Lattice.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(L, \leq)$ be a bounded distributive lattice with top element $\top$ and
bottom element $\bot$. An element $a' \in L$ is a \emph{complement} of
$a \in L$ if
\[
 a \vee a' = \top \quad \text{and} \quad a \wedge a' = \bot.
\]
A \emph{Boolean lattice} (or \emph{Boolean algebra}) is a bounded distributive
lattice in which every element has a complement.

nodes.name: Hasse Diagram
nodes.question: State the definition: Hasse Diagram.
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{Hasse diagram} of a finite poset $(A, \leq)$ is the directed graph
whose vertices are the elements of $A$, with an upward edge from $a$ to $b$
whenever $a \lessdot b$. Three graphical conventions apply:
- [label=(\roman*)]
- Reflexive loops ($a \leq a$) are suppressed.
- Edges implied by transitivity are suppressed: if $a \lessdot b$ and
 $b \lessdot c$, no direct edge from $a$ to $c$ is drawn.
- Direction is encoded by height: $a \lessdot b$ is drawn with $b$
 strictly above $a$, so arrowheads are unnecessary.

nodes.name: Duality Principle for Posets
nodes.question: State the proposition: Duality Principle for Posets.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\Phi$ be any first-order statement about a poset $(A, \leq)$ expressed
using only the relation $\leq$. Let $\Phi^*$ be the statement obtained from
$\Phi$ by replacing every occurrence of $\leq$ with $\geq$ (equivalently,
working in the dual poset). Then:
\[
 (A, \leq) \models \Phi
 \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
 (A, \geq) \models \Phi.
\]
In particular, if $\Phi$ is a theorem about all posets, then so is $\Phi^*$.

nodes.question: State the definition: Variable.

from the distinguished variable stock of \(\mathcal L\). Variables are usually

\]

nodes.name: Well-Formed Formula
nodes.question: State the definition: Well-Formed Formula.
nodes.statement_display:
The set of \emph{well-formed formulas} of a first-order language
\(\mathcal L\), denoted \(\mathsf{Form}_{\mathcal L}\), is the smallest set of
strings satisfying:
- every atomic formula is a well-formed formula;
- if \(\varphi\) is a well-formed formula, then
 \(\neg\varphi\) is a well-formed formula;
- if \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are well-formed formulas and
 \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}\), then
 \((\varphi\circ\psi)\) is a well-formed formula;
- if \(\varphi\) is a well-formed formula and \(x\) is a variable, then
 \(\forall x\,\varphi\) and \(\exists x\,\varphi\) are well-formed
 formulas;
- no string is a well-formed formula unless it is generated by finitely
 many applications of the previous clauses.
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf{Form}_{\mathcal L}
=
\bigcap\{S:\;&
\mathsf{Atom}_{\mathcal L}\subseteq S,\\
&(\forall\varphi\in S)(\neg\varphi\in S),\\
&(\forall\varphi,\psi\in S)
(\forall\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\})
((\varphi\circ\psi)\in S),\\
&(\forall x\in\mathsf{Var}_{\mathcal L})(\forall\varphi\in S)
(\forall x\,\varphi\in S\land \exists x\,\varphi\in S)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf{Form}_{\mathcal L}
=

&(\forall\varphi,\psi\in S)
(\forall\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\})
((\varphi\circ\psi)\in S),\\
&(\forall x\in\mathsf{Var}_{\mathcal L})(\forall\varphi\in S)
(\forall x\,\varphi\in S\land \exists x\,\varphi\in S)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.name: Scope of a Quantifier
nodes.question: State the definition: Scope of a Quantifier.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\varphi$ be a formula of a first-order language.

If $\varphi$ is of the form $\forall x\,\psi$ or $\exists x\,\psi$, then the
formula $\psi$ is called the \emph{scope} of the quantifier.

The quantifier is said to \emph{bind} all occurrences of the variable $x$ that
appear within its scope.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $\varphi$ be a formula of a first-order language.

If $\varphi$ is of the form $\forall x\,\psi$ or $\exists x\,\psi$, then the
formula $\psi$ is called the \emph{scope} of the quantifier.

nodes.statement_display:

An occurrence of $x$ is \emph{free} if it is not bound by any quantifier in
$\varphi$.

nodes.name: Free Variables of a Formula
nodes.question: State the definition: Free Variables of a Formula.
nodes.statement_display:
The set $\mathrm{FV}(\varphi)$ of \emph{free variables} of a formula $\varphi$
is defined recursively:
- If $\varphi = P(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ is atomic, then
 $\mathrm{FV}(\varphi) = \bigcup_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Var}(t_i)$,
 where $\mathrm{Var}(t_i)$ is the set of variables in term $t_i$.
- $\mathrm{FV}(\neg \varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi)$.
- $\mathrm{FV}(\varphi \circ \psi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \cup \mathrm{FV}(\psi)$
 for any binary connective $\circ$.
- $\mathrm{FV}(\forall x\,\varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}$.
- $\mathrm{FV}(\exists x\,\varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}$.
nodes.statement_tex:
The set $\mathrm{FV}(\varphi)$ of \emph{free variables} of a formula $\varphi$
is defined recursively:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item If $\varphi = P(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ is atomic, then
 $\mathrm{FV}(\varphi) = \bigcup_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Var}(t_i)$,
 where $\mathrm{Var}(t_i)$ is the set of variables in term $t_i$.

 \item $\mathrm{FV}(\neg \varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi)$.

 \item $\mathrm{FV}(\varphi \circ \psi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \cup \mathrm{FV}(\psi)$
 for any binary connective $\circ$.

 \item $\mathrm{FV}(\forall x\,\varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}$.

 \item $\mathrm{FV}(\exists x\,\varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement_display:
Let $\varphi$ be a formula, $x$ a variable, and $t$ a term.

The expression $\varphi[t/x]$ denotes the formula obtained from $\varphi$ by
replacing every \emph{free} occurrence of $x$ with the term $t$, leaving bound
occurrences of $x$ unchanged.

nodes.name: Free for Substitution
nodes.question: State the definition: Free for Substitution.
nodes.statement_display:
A term $t$ is \emph{free for} $x$ in $\varphi$ if no free occurrence of $x$ in
$\varphi$ lies within the scope of a quantifier $\forall y$ or $\exists y$
where $y$ is a variable occurring in $t$.

Equivalently, $t$ is free for $x$ in $\varphi$ if the substitution $\varphi[t/x]$
does not result in any variable in $t$ becoming bound.
nodes.statement_tex:
A term $t$ is \emph{free for} $x$ in $\varphi$ if no free occurrence of $x$ in
$\varphi$ lies within the scope of a quantifier $\forall y$ or $\exists y$
where $y$ is a variable occurring in $t$.

Equivalently, $t$ is free for $x$ in $\varphi$ if the substitution $\varphi[t/x]$
does not result in any variable in $t$ becoming bound.
nodes.formal:
The relation ``$t$ is free for $x$ in $\varphi$'' is defined by structural
induction on formulas. It is automatic for atomic formulas. It is preserved
through Boolean connectives:
\[
  t\text{ free for }x\text{ in }\neg\varphi
  \iff
  t\text{ free for }x\text{ in }\varphi,
\]
and similarly componentwise for $\varphi\land\psi$, $\varphi\lor\psi$, and
$\varphi\to\psi$. For a quantified formula, the capture-avoidance condition is
\[
  t\text{ free for }x\text{ in }Qy\,\varphi
  \iff
  \bigl(x\text{ is not free in }Qy\,\varphi\bigr)
  \text{ or }
  \bigl(y\notin\operatorname{Var}(t)
    \text{ and }t\text{ is free for }x\text{ in }\varphi\bigr),
\]
where $Q$ is either $\forall$ or $\exists$.

nodes.name: Alpha-Equivalence
nodes.question: State the definition: Alpha-Equivalence.
nodes.statement_display:
Formulas that differ only by the names of bound variables are logically
equivalent. This is called \emph{alpha-equivalence} (or \emph{alphabetic
variance}):
\[
\forall x\,\varphi \;\equiv\; \forall y\,\varphi[y/x]
\quad\text{(provided $y$ is not free in $\varphi$).}
\]

nodes.name: Formula Depth
nodes.question: State the definition: Formula Depth.
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{depth} (or \emph{complexity}) of a formula $\varphi$, denoted
$\mathrm{depth}(\varphi)$, is a natural number defined recursively:
- \textbf{Atomic case.} If $\varphi$ is atomic, then $\mathrm{depth}(\varphi) = 0$.
- \textbf{Negation.} If $\varphi = \neg \psi$, then
 $\mathrm{depth}(\varphi) = \mathrm{depth}(\psi) + 1$.
- \textbf{Binary connectives.} If $\varphi = (\psi \circ \chi)$
 for $\circ \in \{\wedge,\vee,\rightarrow,\leftrightarrow\}$, then
 \[
 \mathrm{depth}(\varphi) = \max\{\mathrm{depth}(\psi),\,\mathrm{depth}(\chi)\} + 1.
 \]
- \textbf{Quantifiers.} If $\varphi = \forall x\,\psi$ or $\varphi = \exists x\,\psi$,
 then $\mathrm{depth}(\varphi) = \mathrm{depth}(\psi) + 1$.
nodes.statement_tex:

 \item \textbf{Negation.} If $\varphi = \neg \psi$, then

 \item \textbf{Binary connectives.} If $\varphi = (\psi \circ \chi)$

 \[
 \mathrm{depth}(\varphi) = \max\{\mathrm{depth}(\psi),\,\mathrm{depth}(\chi)\} + 1.
 \]

 \item \textbf{Quantifiers.} If $\varphi = \forall x\,\psi$ or $\varphi = \exists x\,\psi$,
 then $\mathrm{depth}(\varphi) = \mathrm{depth}(\psi) + 1$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: First-Order Language
nodes.question: State the definition: First-Order Language.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{first-order language} \(\mathcal L\) consists of variables, logical
symbols, and a signature of non-logical symbols: constant symbols, function
symbols with assigned arities, and predicate symbols with assigned arities.
Equality may be included as a distinguished logical predicate.

nodes.name: Structure
nodes.question: State the definition: Structure.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\mathcal L\) be a first-order language. A \emph{structure} for
\(\mathcal L\) is a pair
\[
\mathcal M=\langle D,I\rangle
\]
where \(D\) is a nonempty set and \(I\) assigns each constant symbol an element
of \(D\), each \(n\)-ary function symbol a function \(D^n\to D\), and each
\(n\)-ary predicate symbol a relation on \(D^n\).

s(y), & y\neq x.
\end{cases}
\]

nodes.name: Term Evaluation
nodes.question: State the definition: Term Evaluation.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\mathcal M=\langle D,I\rangle\) be a structure and \(s\) a variable
assignment. The \emph{value} of a term \(t\), denoted
\(\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}\), is defined recursively by
\[
\llbracket x\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}=s(x),\qquad
\llbracket c\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}=I(c),
\]
and
\[
\llbracket f(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}
=
I(f)\bigl(\llbracket t_1\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s},\ldots,
\llbracket t_n\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}\bigr).
\]

language. The sentence \(\varphi\) is a \emph{logical consequence} of \(T\),
written \(T\models\varphi\), exactly when every model of \(T\) is a model of
\(\varphi\).

\(\varphi\).

nodes.name: Logical Equivalence
nodes.question: State the definition: Logical Equivalence.
nodes.statement_display:
Two sentences \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are \emph{logically equivalent}, written
\(\varphi\equiv\psi\), exactly when each is a logical consequence of the other:
\[
\varphi\models\psi
\quad\text{and}\quad
\psi\models\varphi.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Two sentences \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are \emph{logically equivalent}, written
\(\varphi\equiv\psi\), exactly when each is a logical consequence of the other:
\[
\varphi\models\psi
\quad\text{and}\quad
\psi\models\varphi.
\]
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{LogicalEquivalence}(\varphi,\psi)\) means that \(\varphi\) and
\(\psi\) have the same truth value in every structure.
nodes.formal:
\[
\varphi\equiv\psi
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall \mathcal M\;(\mathcal M\models\varphi \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal M\models\psi).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\varphi\equiv\psi
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall \mathcal M\;(\mathcal M\models\varphi \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal M\models\psi).
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\varphi\not\equiv\psi
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists \mathcal M\;\bigl((\mathcal M\models\varphi \land \mathcal M\not\models\psi)
\lor
(\mathcal M\models\psi \land \mathcal M\not\models\varphi)\bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\varphi\not\equiv\psi
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists \mathcal M\;\bigl((\mathcal M\models\varphi \land \mathcal M\not\models\psi)
\lor
(\mathcal M\models\psi \land \mathcal M\not\models\varphi)\bigr).
\]

nodes.name: Substitution Lemma for Terms
nodes.question: State the lemma: Substitution Lemma for Terms.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\mathcal M\) be a structure, let \(s\) be a variable assignment, let
\(x\) be a variable, and let \(t\) and \(u\) be terms. Then
\[
\llbracket t[u/x]\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}
=
\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,\,
s[x\mapsto\llbracket u\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}]}.
\]

s[x\mapsto\llbracket u\rrbracket_{\mathcal M,s}]}.

\]

nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{bounded quantifier} is an abbreviation that restricts a quantifier to a
specified set or predicate:
\[
\forall x\in A\,\varphi
\quad\coloneqq\quad
\forall x\,(x\in A\to\varphi),
\]
\[
\exists x\in A\,\varphi
\quad\coloneqq\quad
\exists x\,(x\in A\land\varphi).
\]

\[
\exists x\in A\,\varphi
\quad\coloneqq\quad
\exists x\,(x\in A\land\varphi).
\]

restricted universal or existential quantifier.

\[

\exists x\in A\,\varphi \equiv \exists x\,(x\in A\land\varphi).
\]

uses conjunction. This preserves the usual behavior on empty sets.

nodes.name: Renaming Bound Variables
nodes.question: State the theorem: Renaming Bound Variables.
nodes.statement_display:
If \(y\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) and no capture is introduced, then
\[
\forall x\,\varphi\equiv\forall y\,\varphi[y/x],
\qquad
\exists x\,\varphi\equiv\exists y\,\varphi[y/x].
\]

\[
\forall x\,\varphi\equiv\forall y\,\varphi[y/x],
\qquad
\exists x\,\varphi\equiv\exists y\,\varphi[y/x].
\]
nodes.proposition:
Renaming bound variables preserves logical equivalence when the renaming is
capture-avoiding.

\[
y \text{ free for } x \text{ in } \varphi
\Rightarrow
(\forall x\,\varphi\equiv\forall y\,\varphi[y/x])
\land
(\exists x\,\varphi\equiv\exists y\,\varphi[y/x]).
\]

\]

Bound variable names are placeholders. Renaming them changes notation, not
meaning, provided no free variable becomes captured.

nodes.question: State the definition: Quantifier Order.
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{quantifier order} of a prenex formula is the ordered list of
quantifiers in its prefix. A change of order is significant when it changes
which witnesses may depend on earlier variables.

the quantifiers in the prefix of \(\Phi\).

for all \(x\).

\]

nodes.name: Negation Translation Pattern
nodes.question: State the proposition: Negation Translation Pattern.
nodes.statement_display:
The negation of a translated quantified statement is obtained by negating the
whole formula and then pushing the negation inward using the quantifier
negation laws.

\(\operatorname{NegationTranslationPattern}(\varphi,\psi)\) records that
\(\psi\) is obtained from \(\neg\varphi\) by pushing negation through the
quantifiers and connectives.
nodes.source_text:
The negation of ``all'' is ``some not.'' The negation of ``some'' is ``none.''
For restricted universal claims, negating the implication produces a witness
that satisfies the restriction and fails the consequent.

nodes.name: Scope Ambiguity
nodes.question: State the definition: Scope Ambiguity.
nodes.statement_display:
A sentence has \emph{scope ambiguity} when the same ordinary-language wording
admits two or more translations with different quantifier nesting or different
connective scope.
nodes.statement_tex:
A sentence has \emph{scope ambiguity} when the same ordinary-language wording
admits two or more translations with different quantifier nesting or different
connective scope.
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{ScopeAmbiguity}(E,\varphi,\psi)\) means that the English
sentence \(E\) can reasonably be translated by \(\varphi\) or by \(\psi\), and
the difference is a scope difference.
nodes.source_text:
Scope is not cosmetic. Changing the outer quantifier can change whether a
single witness works for everyone or whether each object may have its own
witness.

nodes.name: A-O Contradiction
nodes.question: State the proposition: A-O Contradiction.
nodes.statement_display:
The \(A\)-form \(\forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x))\) and the \(O\)-form
\(\exists x\,(A(x)\land \neg B(x))\) are contradictory: exactly one of them is
true.

\(\exists x\,(A(x)\land \neg B(x))\) are contradictory: exactly one of them is
true.

 \hyperref[prf:a-o-contradictory-predicate-logic]{Go to proof.}

\(A\)-form and \(O\)-form cannot share a truth value.

\Longleftrightarrow

is \(A\) but not \(B\).

\to
\neg\bigl(

\bigr).

\(\neg B\) of that object. Without such an object, both universals may be
vacuously true. The traditional square of opposition assumes existential
import; modern first-order logic does not automatically assume that a universal
statement implies existence.

nodes.name: Logical Connective
nodes.question: State the definition: Logical Connective.
nodes.statement_display:
The standard primitive propositional connectives are
\[
\neg,\qquad \land,\qquad \lor,\qquad \to,\qquad \leftrightarrow.
\]
The connective \(\neg\) is unary. The connectives \(\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\) are binary.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
\text{Symbol} & \text{Name} & \text{Arity} & \text{Formation pattern} & \text{Reading}\\
\hline
\neg & \text{negation} & \text{unary} & \neg\varphi & \text{not }\varphi\\
\land & \text{conjunction} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\land\psi) & \varphi\text{ and }\psi\\
\lor & \text{disjunction} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\lor\psi) & \varphi\text{ or }\psi\\
\to & \text{conditional} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\to\psi) & \text{if }\varphi,\text{ then }\psi\\
\leftrightarrow & \text{biconditional} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi) & \varphi\text{ iff }\psi
\end{array}
\]

\leftrightarrow & \text{biconditional} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi) & \varphi\text{ iff }\psi

nodes.name: Well-Formed Formula
nodes.question: State the definition: Well-Formed Formula.
nodes.statement_display:
The set \(\WFF\) of well-formed formulas is the smallest set of strings satisfying the following formation rules:
- Every propositional variable \(P\in\Prop\) belongs to \(\WFF\).
- If \(\varphi\in\WFF\), then \(\neg\varphi\in\WFF\).
- If \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\) and \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}\), then \((\varphi\circ\psi)\in\WFF\).

nodes.statement_tex:
The set \(\WFF\) of well-formed formulas is the smallest set of strings satisfying the following formation rules:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every propositional variable \(P\in\Prop\) belongs to \(\WFF\).
\item If \(\varphi\in\WFF\), then \(\neg\varphi\in\WFF\).
\item If \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\) and \(\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\}\), then \((\varphi\circ\psi)\in\WFF\).
\item No string is a well-formed formula unless it is obtained by finitely many applications of the previous clauses.
\end{enumerate}

\LRAProofBodyStart
This is exactly the closure part of the recursive definition of
\(\WFF\). If \(\varphi\in\WFF\), then the negation formation rule gives

nodes.name: Formula Depth
nodes.question: State the definition: Formula Depth.
nodes.statement_display:
The depth of a formula \(\varphi\), denoted \(\operatorname{depth}(\varphi)\), is defined recursively:
- if \(\varphi\) is atomic, then \(\operatorname{depth}(\varphi)=0\);
- if \(\varphi=\neg\psi\), then \(\operatorname{depth}(\varphi)=\operatorname{depth}(\psi)+1\);
- if \(\varphi=(\psi\circ\chi)\), then
\[
\operatorname{depth}(\varphi)=\max\{\operatorname{depth}(\psi),\operatorname{depth}(\chi)\}+1.
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{depth}(P)=0,\qquad
\operatorname{depth}(\neg\psi)=\operatorname{depth}(\psi)+1,
\]
\[
\operatorname{depth}((\psi\circ\chi))
=
\max\{\operatorname{depth}(\psi),\operatorname{depth}(\chi)\}+1.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{depth}(P)=0,\qquad
\operatorname{depth}(\neg\psi)=\operatorname{depth}(\psi)+1,
\]
\[
\operatorname{depth}((\psi\circ\chi))
=
\max\{\operatorname{depth}(\psi),\operatorname{depth}(\chi)\}+1.
\]
nodes.source_text: Formula depth measures the height of the syntax tree. Some authors call this the rank, complexity, or formation depth of the formula.

nodes.statement_display:

\]

value assigned to \(P\).

nodes.name: Extension of a Truth Assignment to Formulas
nodes.question: State the definition: Extension of a Truth Assignment to Formulas.
nodes.statement_display:
Let
\[
v:\Prop\to\mathbb{B}
\]
be a truth assignment. The \emph{extension} of \(v\) to well-formed formulas is
the function
\[
\widehat v:\WFF\to\mathbb{B}
\]
defined recursively as follows:
\[
\widehat v(P)=v(P)
\quad\text{for every }P\in\Prop,
\]
\[
\widehat v(\neg\varphi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\False,
\]
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\land\psi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\True
\text{ and }
\widehat v(\psi)=\True,
\]
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\lor\psi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\True
\text{ or }
\widehat v(\psi)=\True,
\]
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\to\psi)=\False
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\True
\text{ and }
\widehat v(\psi)=\False,
\]
and
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\widehat v(\psi).
\]

nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\varphi\in\WFF\) and suppose the variables occurring in \(\varphi\) are among \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\). A truth table for \(\varphi\) is a finite table with one row for each assignment

\]

nodes.name: Coincidence Lemma for Propositional Logic
nodes.question: State the lemma: Coincidence Lemma for Propositional Logic.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(v,w:\Prop\to\mathbb{B}\) be truth assignments. If \(v\) and \(w\) agree on every propositional variable occurring in \(\varphi\), then they assign the same truth value to \(\varphi\):
\[
v|_{\operatorname{Var}(\varphi)}
=
w|_{\operatorname{Var}(\varphi)}
\Longrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\widehat w(\varphi).
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
(\forall\varphi\in\WFF)
(\forall v,w:\Prop\to\mathbb{B})
\left[
(\forall P\in\operatorname{Var}(\varphi))(v(P)=w(P))
\to
\widehat v(\varphi)=\widehat w(\varphi)
\right].
\]

\[

nodes.name: Logical Equivalence is an Equivalence Relation
nodes.question: State the theorem: Logical Equivalence is an Equivalence Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
Logical equivalence is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive on \(\WFF\):
\[
\varphi\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\equiv\psi\Longrightarrow\psi\equiv\varphi,
\]
and
\[
(\varphi\equiv\psi\land\psi\equiv\chi)
\Longrightarrow
\varphi\equiv\chi.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Logical equivalence is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive on \(\WFF\):
\[

\Longrightarrow
\varphi\equiv\chi.
\]

 \hyperref[prf:logical-equivalence-equivalence-relation]{Go to proof.}

\begin{aligned}
&(\forall\varphi\in\WFF)(\varphi\equiv\varphi),\\

&(\forall\varphi,\psi,\chi\in\WFF)

\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.name: Basic Boolean Equivalence Laws
nodes.question: State the theorem: Basic Boolean Equivalence Laws.
nodes.statement_display:
For all formulas \(\varphi,\psi,\chi\in\WFF\), the following logical equivalences hold.

Commutativity:
\[
\varphi\land\psi\equiv\psi\land\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\psi\equiv\psi\lor\varphi.
\]

Associativity:
\[
(\varphi\land\psi)\land\chi
\equiv
\varphi\land(\psi\land\chi),
\qquad
(\varphi\lor\psi)\lor\chi
\equiv
\varphi\lor(\psi\lor\chi).
\]

Idempotence:
\[
\varphi\land\varphi\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\varphi\equiv\varphi.
\]

Double negation:
\[
\neg\neg\varphi\equiv\varphi.
\]

nodes.name: Identity and Domination Laws
nodes.question: State the theorem: Identity and Domination Laws.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\top\) be any tautological formula and let \(\bot\) be any contradictory formula. Then for every \(\varphi\in\WFF\):
\[
\varphi\land\top\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\bot\equiv\varphi,
\]
and
\[
\varphi\land\bot\equiv\bot,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\top\equiv\top.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let \(\top\) be any tautological formula and let \(\bot\) be any contradictory formula. Then for every \(\varphi\in\WFF\):
\[
\varphi\land\top\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\bot\equiv\varphi,
\]
and
\[
\varphi\land\bot\equiv\bot,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\top\equiv\top.
\]

 \hyperref[prf:identity-domination-laws-propositional-logic]{Go to proof.}
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(\operatorname{Tautology}(\top)\land \operatorname{Contradiction}(\bot))
\to
(\forall\varphi\in\WFF)\\
&\quad
\left[
(\varphi\land\top\equiv\varphi)
\land
(\varphi\lor\bot\equiv\varphi)
\land
(\varphi\land\bot\equiv\bot)
\land
(\varphi\lor\top\equiv\top)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(\operatorname{Tautology}(\top)\land \operatorname{Contradiction}(\bot))
\to
(\forall\varphi\in\WFF)\\
&\quad
\left[
(\varphi\land\top\equiv\varphi)
\land
(\varphi\lor\bot\equiv\varphi)
\land
(\varphi\land\bot\equiv\bot)
\land
(\varphi\lor\top\equiv\top)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.name: Biconditional Equivalence Laws
nodes.question: State the theorem: Biconditional Equivalence Laws.
nodes.statement_display:
For all \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\),
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\to\psi)\land(\psi\to\varphi),
\]
and
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\land\psi)\lor(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
For all \(\varphi,\psi\in\WFF\),
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\to\psi)\land(\psi\to\varphi),
\]
and
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\land\psi)\lor(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi).
\]

 \hyperref[prf:biconditional-equivalence-laws-propositional-logic]{Go to proof.}
nodes.proposition:
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(\varphi\to\psi)\land(\psi\to\varphi)
\]
and also
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(\varphi\land\psi)\lor(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi).
\]
The biconditional says that the two formulas have the same truth value.

nodes.question: State the theorem: Replacement of Logical Equivalents.
nodes.statement_display:
Replacing logically equivalent formulas inside a formula context preserves logical equivalence:
\[
\varphi\equiv\psi
\Longrightarrow
C[\varphi]\equiv C[\psi].
\]

\Longrightarrow
C[\varphi]\equiv C[\psi].
\]

 \hyperref[prf:replacement-of-logical-equivalents-propositional-logic]{Go to proof.}
nodes.proposition:
\[
\varphi\equiv\psi
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
C[\varphi]\equiv C[\psi].
\]
A logical equivalence may be used inside a larger formula context without changing
the truth behavior of the whole formula.

\right].

nodes.name: Literal
nodes.question: State the definition: Literal.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{literal} is either a propositional variable \(P\) or the negation
\(\neg P\) of a propositional variable \(P\).

atomic propositional variable.
nodes.formal:

\[
\ell\text{ is a literal}
\Longleftrightarrow
(\exists P\in\Prop)(\ell=P\text{ or }\ell=\neg P).
\]

Literals are the indivisible signed atoms used in normal forms. They remember
which propositional variable is being tested and whether it appears positively
or negatively.

nodes.name: Complementary Literals
nodes.question: State the definition: Complementary Literals.
nodes.statement_display:
Two literals are \emph{complementary} if they are \(P\) and \(\neg P\) for the
same propositional variable \(P\).
nodes.statement_tex:
Two literals are \emph{complementary} if they are \(P\) and \(\neg P\) for the
same propositional variable \(P\).
nodes.proposition:
\[
\operatorname{ComplementaryLiterals}(\ell_1,\ell_2)
\]
means that the two literals name the same propositional variable with opposite
signs.
nodes.formal:
For literals \(\ell_1,\ell_2\),
\[
\ell_1\text{ and }\ell_2\text{ are complementary}
\Longleftrightarrow
(\exists P\in\Prop)
\bigl((\ell_1=P\land \ell_2=\neg P)
\lor
(\ell_1=\neg P\land \ell_2=P)\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
For literals \(\ell_1,\ell_2\),
\[
\ell_1\text{ and }\ell_2\text{ are complementary}
\Longleftrightarrow
(\exists P\in\Prop)
\bigl((\ell_1=P\land \ell_2=\neg P)
\lor
(\ell_1=\neg P\land \ell_2=P)\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Complementary literals are the local contradiction pattern inside clauses and
terms. The pair \(P,\neg P\) is tied to one variable, not merely to two formulas
with opposite truth values under a particular assignment.

nodes.name: Clause
nodes.question: State the definition: Clause.
nodes.statement_display: A \emph{clause} is a finite disjunction of literals.
nodes.statement_tex: A \emph{clause} is a finite disjunction of literals.
nodes.proposition:
\[
\operatorname{Clause}(C)
\]
means that \(C\) is built by finitely disjoining literals.
nodes.formal:
A formula \(C\in\WFF\) is a clause if there are literals
\(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n\) with \(n\ge 1\) such that
\[
C=\ell_1\lor\cdots\lor\ell_n.
\]
The empty clause is treated separately as the empty disjunction.
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
A formula \(C\in\WFF\) is a clause if there are literals
\(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n\) with \(n\ge 1\) such that
\[
C=\ell_1\lor\cdots\lor\ell_n.
\]
The empty clause is treated separately as the empty disjunction.
nodes.source_text:
A clause records a finite list of literal-level alternatives. It is satisfied
when at least one of its literals is true.

nodes.statement_display:
A formula is in \emph{negation normal form} if it uses only propositional
variables, negated propositional variables, conjunction, and disjunction, and
every negation occurs immediately before a propositional variable.

nodes.name: NNF Conversion Procedure
nodes.question: State the definition: NNF Conversion Procedure.
nodes.proposition:
\[
\operatorname{NNFConversionProcedure}(\varphi,\psi)
\]
means that \(\psi\) is obtained from \(\varphi\) by eliminating
biconditionals and conditionals, removing double negations, and pushing
remaining negations inward.
nodes.formal:
Starting with \(\varphi\in\WFF\), repeatedly apply the equivalences
\[
\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta
\equiv
(\alpha\to\beta)\land(\beta\to\alpha),
\qquad
\alpha\to\beta\equiv\neg\alpha\lor\beta,
\]
\[
\neg\neg\alpha\equiv\alpha,
\qquad
\neg(\alpha\land\beta)\equiv\neg\alpha\lor\neg\beta,
\qquad
\neg(\alpha\lor\beta)\equiv\neg\alpha\land\neg\beta,
\]
until negations occur only immediately before propositional variables and only
\(\land\) and \(\lor\) remain above the literal level.
nodes.fully_quantified_form:

\[

\]
\[

\qquad

\qquad
\neg(\alpha\lor\beta)\equiv\neg\alpha\land\neg\beta,
\]
until negations occur only immediately before propositional variables and only
\(\land\) and \(\lor\) remain above the literal level.
nodes.source_text:
The procedure is a syntax-directed rewrite process. Each rewrite step is backed
by a logical equivalence law, so the output formula has the same truth
conditions as the input formula.

Let \(\varphi\in\WFF\), and fix an ordering \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) of the finite
variable set of \(\varphi\). The \emph{canonical disjunctive normal form} of
\(\varphi\) relative to this ordering is the disjunction of the

corresponding to the rows on which \(\varphi\) is true.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let \(\varphi\in\WFF\), and fix an ordering \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) of the finite
variable set of \(\varphi\). The \emph{canonical disjunctive normal form} of
\(\varphi\) relative to this ordering is the disjunction of the

corresponding to the rows on which \(\varphi\) is true.
nodes.formal:
For \(\mathrm{Var}(\varphi)=\{P_1,\ldots,P_n\}\), the canonical
disjunctive normal form is
\[
\bigvee_{\widehat v(\varphi)=\True}
\bigl(L_1\land\cdots\land L_n\bigr),
\]

nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\varphi\in\WFF\), and fix an ordering \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) of the finite
variable set of \(\varphi\). The \emph{canonical conjunctive normal form} of
\(\varphi\) relative to this ordering is the conjunction of the

corresponding to the rows on which \(\varphi\) is false.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let \(\varphi\in\WFF\), and fix an ordering \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) of the finite
variable set of \(\varphi\). The \emph{canonical conjunctive normal form} of
\(\varphi\) relative to this ordering is the conjunction of the

corresponding to the rows on which \(\varphi\) is false.

\[
\bigwedge_{\widehat v(\varphi)=\False}

nodes.source_text:
Canonical CNF records exactly the truth-table rows on which the formula is

nodes.name: Representation of a Boolean Function
nodes.question: State the definition: Representation of a Boolean Function.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\) be a Boolean function. A formula
\(\varphi\in\WFF\) with variables among \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) \emph{represents}
\(f\) if for every truth assignment \(v\),
\[
\widehat v(\varphi)=f(v(P_1),\ldots,v(P_n)).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\) be a Boolean function. A formula
\(\varphi\in\WFF\) with variables among \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\) \emph{represents}
\(f\) if for every truth assignment \(v\),
\[
\widehat v(\varphi)=f(v(P_1),\ldots,v(P_n)).
\]
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n)\) means that
\(\varphi\) has exactly the same truth table as the Boolean function \(f\) on
the listed variables.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall v:\Prop\to\mathbb{B})
\bigl(\widehat v(\varphi)=f(v(P_1),\ldots,v(P_n))\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall v:\Prop\to\mathbb{B})
\bigl(\widehat v(\varphi)=f(v(P_1),\ldots,v(P_n))\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text:
A formula represents a Boolean function when the formula computes the same
truth value as the function for every input row. This turns a semantic table of
values into a syntactic object inside the propositional language.

nodes.name: DNF Representation of Boolean Functions
nodes.question: State the theorem: DNF Representation of Boolean Functions.
nodes.statement_display:
Every Boolean function \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\) is represented by a
formula in disjunctive normal form using variables \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\).
nodes.proposition:
Every \(n\)-ary Boolean function has a propositional formula representative, and
one may choose the representative to be in disjunctive normal form.
nodes.formal:
\[
(\forall f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B})(\exists\varphi\in\WFF)
\bigl(\varphi\text{ is in DNF}\land
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n)\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
(\forall f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B})(\exists\varphi\in\WFF)
\bigl(\varphi\text{ is in DNF}\land
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n)\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text:
A truth table specifies which input rows make the Boolean function true. For
each true row, form the corresponding conjunction of literals; the disjunction
of those row conjunctions represents the entire function.

nodes.name: Functionally Complete Connective Set
nodes.question: State the definition: Functionally Complete Connective Set.
nodes.statement_display:
A connective basis \(B\) is \emph{functionally complete} if every Boolean
function \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\), for every \(n\ge 1\), is represented
by some formula using only connectives from \(B\).
nodes.statement_tex:
A connective basis \(B\) is \emph{functionally complete} if every Boolean
function \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\), for every \(n\ge 1\), is represented
by some formula using only connectives from \(B\).
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(B)\) means that formulas over \(B\) can
represent every finite Boolean input-output table.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(B)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall n\ge 1)(\forall f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B})(\exists\varphi\in\WFF_B)
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(B)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall n\ge 1)(\forall f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B})(\exists\varphi\in\WFF_B)
\operatorname{Represents}(\varphi,f;P_1,\ldots,P_n).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Functional completeness is the central expressive-power property for connective
sets. It says that the basis can express all possible truth-functional behavior,
not merely the connectives originally listed in the language.

nodes.name: Expressively Equivalent Connective Sets
nodes.question: State the definition: Expressively Equivalent Connective Sets.
nodes.statement_display:
Two connective bases \(B\) and \(C\) are \emph{expressively equivalent} if every
connective in \(B\) is definable from \(C\), and every connective in \(C\) is
definable from \(B\).
nodes.statement_tex:
Two connective bases \(B\) and \(C\) are \emph{expressively equivalent} if every
connective in \(B\) is definable from \(C\), and every connective in \(C\) is
definable from \(B\).
nodes.proposition:
\(B\equiv_{\mathrm{expr}} C\) means that the two bases can define exactly the
same connective behavior.
nodes.formal:
\[
B\equiv_{\mathrm{expr}} C
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl((\forall\circ\in B)\operatorname{DefinableFrom}(\circ,C)\bigr)
\land
\bigl((\forall\star\in C)\operatorname{DefinableFrom}(\star,B)\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
B\equiv_{\mathrm{expr}} C
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl((\forall\circ\in B)\operatorname{DefinableFrom}(\circ,C)\bigr)
\land
\bigl((\forall\star\in C)\operatorname{DefinableFrom}(\star,B)\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Expressive equivalence lets a proof replace one primitive vocabulary with
another. This is why a language can be simplified syntactically without changing
which truth functions can be expressed.

nodes.name: Negation and Conjunction are Functionally Complete
nodes.question: State the theorem: Negation and Conjunction are Functionally Complete.
nodes.statement_display:
The connective basis
\[
\{\neg,\land\}
\]
is functionally complete.
nodes.proposition:
Every Boolean function is represented by a formula using only negation and
conjunction.

\[
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(\{\neg,\land\}).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(\{\neg,\land\}).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Disjunction is definable from negation and conjunction by De Morgan's law:
\[
\varphi\lor\psi\equiv\neg(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi).
\]
Thus every formula using \(\neg,\land,\lor\) can be translated into an equivalent
formula using only \(\neg\) and \(\land\).

nodes.question: State the definition: Connective Reduction.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{connective reduction} replaces a formula using one connective basis by
a logically equivalent formula using a smaller or different connective basis.
nodes.statement_tex:
A \emph{connective reduction} replaces a formula using one connective basis by
a logically equivalent formula using a smaller or different connective basis.
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{Reduction}_{B\to C}(\varphi,\psi)\) means that \(\psi\) is a
translation of \(\varphi\) into the connective basis \(C\) without changing truth
behavior.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{Reduction}_{B\to C}(\varphi,\psi)
\Longleftrightarrow
\varphi\equiv\psi
\quad\text{and}\quad
\psi\in\WFF_C.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{Reduction}_{B\to C}(\varphi,\psi)
\Longleftrightarrow
\varphi\equiv\psi
\quad\text{and}\quad
\psi\in\WFF_C.
\]
nodes.source_text:
Reduction shows that some primitive connectives are optional. If a connective is
definable from the remaining basis, then formulas using that connective can be
translated away.

nodes.name: NAND Connective
nodes.question: State the definition: NAND Connective.
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{NAND} connective, written \(\uparrow\), is the binary connective
defined by
\[
\varphi\uparrow\psi\equiv\neg(\varphi\land\psi).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
The \emph{NAND} connective, written \(\uparrow\), is the binary connective
defined by
\[
\varphi\uparrow\psi\equiv\neg(\varphi\land\psi).
\]
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{NAND}(\varphi,\psi)\) means the negation of the conjunction of
\(\varphi\) and \(\psi\).
nodes.formal:
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\uparrow\psi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{not both }\widehat v(\varphi)=\True\text{ and }\widehat v(\psi)=\True.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\uparrow\psi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{not both }\widehat v(\varphi)=\True\text{ and }\widehat v(\psi)=\True.
\]
nodes.source_text:
NAND is read as "not both." It is false only when both inputs are true. This
single connective can reproduce negation, conjunction, and disjunction.

nodes.name: Monotone Boolean Function
nodes.question: State the definition: Monotone Boolean Function.
nodes.statement_display:
A Boolean function \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\) is \emph{monotone} if
changing input coordinates from \(\False\) to \(\True\) never changes the output
from \(\True\) to \(\False\).
nodes.statement_tex:
A Boolean function \(f:\mathbb{B}^n\to\mathbb{B}\) is \emph{monotone} if
changing input coordinates from \(\False\) to \(\True\) never changes the output
from \(\True\) to \(\False\).
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{Monotone}(f)\) means that increasing truth inputs cannot make the
output decrease from true to false.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{Monotone}(f)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall a,b\in\mathbb{B}^n)
\bigl(a\le b\to f(a)\le f(b)\bigr),
\]
where \(\False\le\True\) coordinatewise.
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{Monotone}(f)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall a,b\in\mathbb{B}^n)
\bigl(a\le b\to f(a)\le f(b)\bigr),
\]
where \(\False\le\True\) coordinatewise.
nodes.source_text:
The connectives \(\land\) and \(\lor\) are monotone. Negation is not monotone,
because changing \(P\) from false to true changes \(\neg P\) from true to false.

nodes.name: Conjunction and Disjunction are not Functionally Complete
nodes.question: State the theorem: Conjunction and Disjunction are not Functionally Complete.
nodes.statement_display: The connective basis \(\{\land,\lor\}\) is not functionally complete.

The connective basis \(\{\land,\lor\}\) is not functionally complete.

 \hyperref[prf:conjunction-disjunction-not-functionally-complete-propositional-logic]{Go to proof.}
nodes.proposition:
There is at least one Boolean function that cannot be represented by any formula
using only conjunction and disjunction.

\[
\neg\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(\{\land,\lor\}).
\]

\neg\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(\{\land,\lor\}).

Boolean function. Since negation is not monotone, no formula using only
\(\land\) and \(\lor\) can represent negation. Hence the basis is incomplete.

nodes.name: Minimal Complete Basis
nodes.question: State the definition: Minimal Complete Basis.
nodes.statement_display:
A functionally complete connective basis \(B\) is \emph{minimal complete} if no
proper subset of \(B\) is functionally complete.
nodes.statement_tex:
A functionally complete connective basis \(B\) is \emph{minimal complete} if no
proper subset of \(B\) is functionally complete.
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{MinimalComplete}(B)\) means that \(B\) is complete, but removing
any primitive connective from \(B\) destroys completeness.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{MinimalComplete}(B)
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(B)
\land
(\forall C\subsetneq B)\neg\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(C).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{MinimalComplete}(B)
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(B)
\land
(\forall C\subsetneq B)\neg\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(C).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Minimality is relative to deletion of connectives from the basis. It does not
mean that formulas using the basis are short or easy to read.
used_by_titles: NAND and NOR are Minimal Complete Bases

nodes.statement_display:
The one-connective bases \(\{\uparrow\}\) and \(\{\downarrow\}\) are minimal
complete bases.
nodes.proposition:
NAND alone is complete, NOR alone is complete, and deleting the sole connective
from either basis leaves no functionally complete basis.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{MinimalComplete}(\{\uparrow\})
\land
\operatorname{MinimalComplete}(\{\downarrow\}).
\]

\operatorname{MinimalComplete}(\{\uparrow\})
\land
\operatorname{MinimalComplete}(\{\downarrow\}).
\]

A one-connective complete basis is automatically minimal once the empty basis is
not functionally complete. NAND and NOR are therefore minimal complete bases
because each is complete by itself.

An \emph{argument form} is a schematic pattern consisting of a finite list of
premise formulas and one conclusion formula.

nodes.name: Valid Argument Form
nodes.question: State the definition: Valid Argument Form.
nodes.statement_display:
An argument form with premises \(\Gamma\) and conclusion \(\varphi\) is
\emph{valid} if every truth assignment that satisfies every formula in
\(\Gamma\) also satisfies \(\varphi\).
nodes.statement_tex:
An argument form with premises \(\Gamma\) and conclusion \(\varphi\) is
\emph{valid} if every truth assignment that satisfies every formula in
\(\Gamma\) also satisfies \(\varphi\).
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)\) means that truth of all
premises forces truth of the conclusion under every truth assignment.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall v)\bigl((\forall\gamma\in\Gamma)(v\models\gamma)
\to v\models\varphi\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall v)\bigl((\forall\gamma\in\Gamma)(v\models\gamma)
\to v\models\varphi\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Validity is a preservation property. A valid argument form may have false
premises in a particular instance, but it cannot have true premises and a false
conclusion under the same truth assignment.

nodes.name: Counterexample Assignment
nodes.question: State the definition: Counterexample Assignment.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{counterexample assignment} to an argument form \((\Gamma,\varphi)\) is a
truth assignment that satisfies every premise in \(\Gamma\) and does not satisfy
\(\varphi\).
nodes.statement_tex:
A \emph{counterexample assignment} to an argument form \((\Gamma,\varphi)\) is a
truth assignment that satisfies every premise in \(\Gamma\) and does not satisfy
\(\varphi\).
nodes.proposition:
\(\operatorname{CounterexampleAssignment}(v,\Gamma,\varphi)\) means that \(v\)
shows the premises can all be true while the conclusion is false.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{CounterexampleAssignment}(v,\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall\gamma\in\Gamma)(v\models\gamma)\land v\not\models\varphi.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{CounterexampleAssignment}(v,\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall\gamma\in\Gamma)(v\models\gamma)\land v\not\models\varphi.
\]
nodes.source_text:
A counterexample assignment is the semantic witness to invalidity. Finding one
settles the question: the argument form is not truth-preserving.

nodes.name: Truth-Table Validity Test for Argument Forms
nodes.question: State the theorem: Truth-Table Validity Test for Argument Forms.
nodes.statement_display:
An argument form \((\Gamma,\varphi)\) is valid if and only if no row of its truth
table makes every formula in \(\Gamma\) true and \(\varphi\) false.
nodes.proposition:
The argument form is valid exactly when there is no counterexample truth
assignment.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
\neg(\exists v)\operatorname{CounterexampleAssignment}(v,\Gamma,\varphi).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{ValidArgumentForm}(\Gamma,\varphi)
\Longleftrightarrow
\neg(\exists v)\operatorname{CounterexampleAssignment}(v,\Gamma,\varphi).
\]
nodes.source_text:
The truth-table test is finite because only the variables appearing in the
premises and conclusion matter. A failed row is a counterexample assignment; the
absence of such rows proves semantic validity.

nodes.name: Replacement Rules Preserve Logical Equivalence
nodes.question: State the theorem: Replacement Rules Preserve Logical Equivalence.
nodes.statement_display:
If a formula \(\psi\) is obtained from a formula \(\varphi\) by finitely many
applications of rules of replacement, then \(\varphi\equiv\psi\).

A finite sequence of equivalence-preserving replacements preserves logical
equivalence from the first formula to the last formula.

\]

\]
nodes.source_text:
Replacement rules justify algebraic manipulation of formulas. Each local rewrite
preserves truth under every truth assignment, so the entire finite rewrite chain
also preserves truth under every truth assignment.

nodes.name: Satisfiable Set of Propositional Formulas
nodes.question: State the definition: Satisfiable Set of Propositional Formulas.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\Gamma\subseteq\WFF\). The set \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable if there exists a
truth assignment \(v\) such that \(v\models\Gamma\).
\[
\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists v\,\bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\land v\models\Gamma\bigr).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let \(\Gamma\subseteq\WFF\). The set \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable if there exists a
truth assignment \(v\) such that \(v\models\Gamma\).
\[
\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists v\,\bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\land v\models\Gamma\bigr).
\]
nodes.proposition:
\[
\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\]
means that one truth assignment makes every formula in \(\Gamma\) true.
nodes.formal:
\[
\Gamma\text{ is satisfiable}
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists v\,\Bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\land
\forall\varphi\in\Gamma\,(\widehat v(\varphi)=\mathrm{True})\Bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\Gamma\text{ is satisfiable}
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists v\,\Bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\land
\forall\varphi\in\Gamma\,(\widehat v(\varphi)=\mathrm{True})\Bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\neg\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall v\,\Bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\Rightarrow
\exists\varphi\in\Gamma\,(\widehat v(\varphi)=\mathrm{False})\Bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\neg\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall v\,\Bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\Rightarrow
\exists\varphi\in\Gamma\,(\widehat v(\varphi)=\mathrm{False})\Bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_predicate:
\[
\neg\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\]
means that every truth assignment fails on at least one formula in \(\Gamma\).
nodes.failure_modes:
Satisfiability fails when every truth assignment is blocked by at least one
formula in \(\Gamma\).
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\neg\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall v\,\Bigl(\operatorname{TruthAssignment}(v)\Rightarrow
\exists\varphi\in\Gamma\,(\widehat v(\varphi)=\mathrm{False})\Bigr).
\]
Thus \(\Gamma\) is not satisfiable exactly when every truth assignment is
defeated by at least one formula from \(\Gamma\).
nodes.source_text:
Satisfiability of a set is a compatibility condition. The formulas in
\(\Gamma\) may impose many requirements, but they are satisfiable only if all
of those requirements can be met by the same truth assignment.

nodes.name: Finitely Satisfiable Set of Propositional Formulas
nodes.question: State the definition: Finitely Satisfiable Set of Propositional Formulas.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\Gamma\subseteq\WFF\). The set \(\Gamma\) is finitely satisfiable if every
finite subset of \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable.
\[
\operatorname{FinitelySatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall\Delta\,\Bigl((\Delta\subseteq\Gamma\land \Delta\text{ is finite})
\Rightarrow \operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Delta)\Bigr).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:

finite subset of \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable.
\[

\Rightarrow \operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Delta)\Bigr).

\]

\]

nodes.failure_modes:

nodes.name: Propositional Compactness
nodes.question: State the theorem: Propositional Compactness.
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(\Gamma\subseteq\WFF\). If every finite subset of \(\Gamma\) is
satisfiable, then \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable.

\operatorname{FinitelySatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Rightarrow
\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\]
means that passing every finite satisfiability test is enough to produce a
truth assignment for all of \(\Gamma\).

\[
\operatorname{FinitelySatisfiableSet}(\Gamma)
\Rightarrow
\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma).
\]

\Rightarrow
\operatorname{SatisfiableSet}(\Gamma).
\]

\Rightarrow

\]
Compactness says that unsatisfiability cannot first appear only at the infinite
level.

Propositional compactness turns infinitely many finite checks into one global
truth assignment. Equivalently, every propositional inconsistency has a finite
witness.

nodes.name: Relation
nodes.question: State the definition: Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{relation} from $A$ to $B$ is any subset $R \subseteq A \times B$.

If $(a,b) \in R$ we write $a \, R \, b$ and say ``$a$ is related to $b$.''
When $A = B$ we say $R$ is a \emph{relation on $A$}.

nodes.name: Reflexive Relation
nodes.question: State the definition: Reflexive Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
A binary relation $R\subseteq A\times A$ is \emph{reflexive} on $A$ if every
element of the domain is related to itself:
\[
 \forall a\in A,\ (a,a)\in R.
\]
In infix notation, this is the condition $\forall a\in A,\ aRa$.
nodes.statement_tex:

\[

nodes.formal:
Reflexivity is a universal requirement over the whole domain:
\[
  \operatorname{Reflexive}_A(R)
  \iff
  \forall a\in A,\ (a,a)\in R.
\]
For first-order logic with equality, the corresponding logical baseline is
the identity axiom
\[
  \forall x\,(x=x),
\]
which forces equality to behave reflexively in every structure.

nodes.name: Irreflexive Relation
nodes.question: State the definition: Irreflexive Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
A binary relation $R\subseteq A\times A$ is \emph{irreflexive} on $A$ if no
element of the domain is related to itself:
\[
 \forall a\in A,\ (a,a)\notin R.
\]
In infix notation, this is the condition $\forall a\in A,\ \neg(aRa)$.
nodes.statement_tex:
A binary relation $R\subseteq A\times A$ is \emph{irreflexive} on $A$ if no
element of the domain is related to itself:
\[
 \forall a\in A,\ (a,a)\notin R.
\]
In infix notation, this is the condition $\forall a\in A,\ \neg(aRa)$.
nodes.formal:
Irreflexivity is not the same as merely failing to be reflexive:
\[
  \operatorname{Irreflexive}_A(R)
  \iff
  \forall a\in A,\ \neg(aRa),
\]
whereas
\[
  \neg\operatorname{Reflexive}_A(R)
  \iff
  \exists a\in A,\ \neg(aRa).
\]
Thus a relation may be neither reflexive nor irreflexive. In first-order
axiomatizations of strict order, irreflexivity is commonly imposed by the
axiom
\[
  \forall x\,\neg(x<x).
\]

nodes.name: Symmetric Relation
nodes.question: State the definition: Symmetric Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
A binary relation $R\subseteq A\times A$ is \emph{symmetric} on $A$ if every
related pair also appears in the reverse order:
\[
 \forall a,b\in A,\ (a,b)\in R \rightarrow (b,a)\in R.
\]
In infix notation, this is $\forall a,b\in A,\ aRb\rightarrow bRa$.
nodes.statement_tex:
A binary relation $R\subseteq A\times A$ is \emph{symmetric} on $A$ if every
related pair also appears in the reverse order:
\[
 \forall a,b\in A,\ (a,b)\in R \rightarrow (b,a)\in R.
\]
In infix notation, this is $\forall a,b\in A,\ aRb\rightarrow bRa$.
nodes.formal:
Symmetry is a conditional property:
\[
  \operatorname{Symmetric}_A(R)
  \iff
  \forall a,b\in A,\ (aRb\rightarrow bRa).
\]
It does not require every pair to be related; it requires only that any
existing directed relation can be reversed. For first-order logic with
equality, symmetry is expressed by the identity axiom
\[
  \forall x\forall y\,(x=y\rightarrow y=x).
\]

nodes.name: Antisymmetric Relation
nodes.question: State the definition: Antisymmetric Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
A binary relation $R\subseteq A\times A$ is \emph{antisymmetric} on $A$ if any
two elements related in both directions must be equal:
\[
 \forall a,b\in A,\;
 \bigl((a,b)\in R\land(b,a)\in R\bigr)\rightarrow a=b.
\]
In infix notation, this is
$\forall a,b\in A,\ ((aRb\land bRa)\rightarrow a=b)$.

nodes.question: State the definition: Asymmetric Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
A binary relation $R\subseteq A\times A$ is \emph{asymmetric} on $A$ if every
related pair excludes the reverse pair:
\[
 \forall a,b\in A,\;
 (a,b)\in R \rightarrow (b,a)\notin R.
\]
In infix notation, this is
$\forall a,b\in A,\ (aRb\rightarrow\neg(bRa))$.

nodes.formal:
Asymmetry is the strict one-way condition
\[
  \operatorname{Asymmetric}_A(R)
  \iff
  \forall a,b\in A,\ (aRb\rightarrow\neg(bRa)).
\]
It implies irreflexivity by taking $a=b$, and it implies antisymmetry because
two-way relation between distinct elements is impossible. Conversely, a
relation that is both irreflexive and antisymmetric is asymmetric. For strict
orders, the typical first-order axiom is
\[
  \forall x\forall y\,(x<y\rightarrow\neg(y<x)).
\]

nodes.question: State the definition: Transitive Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
A binary relation $R\subseteq A\times A$ is \emph{transitive} on $A$ if any
two composable related pairs collapse to a direct related pair:
\[
 \forall a,b,c\in A,\;
 \bigl((a,b)\in R\land(b,c)\in R\bigr)\rightarrow(a,c)\in R.
\]
In infix notation, this is
$\forall a,b,c\in A,\ ((aRb\land bRc)\rightarrow aRc)$.

nodes.formal:
Transitivity is the formal chaining law:
\[
  \operatorname{Transitive}_A(R)
  \iff
  \forall a,b,c\in A,\ ((aRb\land bRc)\rightarrow aRc).
\]
For equality, the corresponding first-order axiom is
\[
  \forall x\forall y\forall z\,((x=y\land y=z)\rightarrow x=z).
\]
Together with reflexivity and symmetry, transitivity gives equivalence
relations; together with reflexivity and antisymmetry, it gives partial
orders.

nodes.name: Universal Property of the Quotient Map
nodes.question: State the theorem: Universal Property of the Quotient Map.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $R$ be an equivalence relation on $A$, let $\pi : A \to A/R$ be the
canonical surjection, and let $f : A \to B$ be any function. Then $f$ is
\emph{constant on equivalence classes} --- meaning $(a,b) \in R$ implies
$f(a) = f(b)$ --- if and only if there exists a unique function
$\bar{f} : A/R \to B$ such that
\[
f = \bar{f} \circ \pi.
\]
When it exists, $\bar{f}$ is defined by $\bar{f}([a]) = f(a)$.

$f \subseteq A \times B$ such that:

- (\emph{Existence / left-total}) for every $a \in A$, there exists $b \in B$
 with $(a,b) \in f$;
- (\emph{Uniqueness / right-unique}) if $(a,b_1) \in f$ and $(a,b_2) \in f$
 then $b_1 = b_2$.
If $(a,b) \in f$ we write $f(a) = b$.

- If $g \circ f$ is surjective, then $g$ is surjective.

- $f^{-1}(S^c) = (f^{-1}(S))^c$.

nodes.name: Set and Membership
nodes.question: State the definition: Set and Membership.
nodes.statement_display:
In axiomatic set theory, the notions of \emph{set} and \emph{membership} are
\emph{primitive}.

- A \emph{set} is an object.
- \emph{Membership} is a binary relation, denoted by $\in$, between objects.

If $x$ is an object and $A$ is a set, the statement $x \in A$ is read as
``$x$ is an element of $A$.'' No definition of ``set'' or ``$\in$'' is given
in more basic terms. Their meaning is determined entirely by the axioms
governing them.
nodes.statement_tex:
In axiomatic set theory, the notions of \emph{set} and \emph{membership} are

\begin{itemize}
 \item A \emph{set} is an object.
 \item \emph{Membership} is a binary relation, denoted by $\in$, between objects.
\end{itemize}

If $x$ is an object and $A$ is a set, the statement $x \in A$ is read as
``$x$ is an element of $A$.'' No definition of ``set'' or ``$\in$'' is given
in more basic terms. Their meaning is determined entirely by the axioms
governing them.

\]

nodes.name: FIP--Cover Duality
nodes.question: State the proposition: FIP--Cover Duality.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $X$ be a set, $A \subseteq X$, and $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in I}$ a
family of subsets of $X$. Let $F_\alpha = U_\alpha^c = X \setminus U_\alpha$.
Then:
\[
\{U_\alpha\} \text{ covers } A
\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\{F_\alpha \cap A\}_{\alpha \in I} \text{ does \emph{not} have the FIP}.
\]
More precisely: the family $\{U_\alpha\}$ does \emph{not} cover $A$ if and
only if the family of closed complements $\{F_\alpha\}$ has the FIP relative
to $A$.

\]

nodes.name: Positive cone
nodes.question: State the definition: Positive cone.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $K$ be an arithmetic system with addition, multiplication, and zero. A
subset $P\subset K$ is called a \emph{positive cone} if it satisfies:
- if $a,b\in P$, then $a+b\in P$;
- if $a,b\in P$, then $ab\in P$;
- for every $a\in K$, exactly one of the following holds:
 \[
 a\in P,
 \qquad
 a=0,
 \qquad
 -a\in P.
 \]
The strict order associated to $P$ is
\[
a<b \iff b-a\in P.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $K$ be an arithmetic system with addition, multiplication, and zero. A
subset $P\subset K$ is called a \emph{positive cone} if it satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item if $a,b\in P$, then $a+b\in P$;
 \item if $a,b\in P$, then $ab\in P$;
 \item for every $a\in K$, exactly one of the following holds:
 \[
 a\in P,
 \qquad
 a=0,
 \qquad
 -a\in P.
 \]
\end{enumerate}
The strict order associated to $P$ is
\[
a<b \iff b-a\in P.
\]

nodes.name: Congruence Modulo an Integer Is an Equivalence Relation
nodes.question: State the theorem: Congruence Modulo an Integer Is an Equivalence Relation.
nodes.statement_display:

symmetric, and transitive on \(\mathbb{Z}\).
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
For each positive integer \(n\), congruence modulo \(n\) is reflexive,
symmetric, and transitive on \(\mathbb{Z}\).
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}
Fix positive \(n\). Reflexivity holds because \(a-a=0=n\cdot 0\). Symmetry
holds because if \(a-b=nk\), then \(b-a=n(-k)\). Transitivity holds because
if \(a-b=nk\) and \(b-c=n\ell\), then \(a-c=(a-b)+(b-c)=n(k+\ell)\). Thus
congruence modulo \(n\) is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
nodes.proof_idea:
The three equivalence-relation laws are divisibility calculations in
\(\mathbb{Z}\).
nodes.source_text:
This permits the quotient set \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) to be formed from
congruence classes.

nodes.name: Modular Addition and Multiplication Are Well-Defined
nodes.question: State the theorem: Modular Addition and Multiplication Are Well-Defined.
nodes.statement_display:
For each positive integer \(n\), addition and multiplication modulo \(n\) are
well-defined operations on \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\).
nodes.statement_tex:
For each positive integer \(n\), addition and multiplication modulo \(n\) are
well-defined operations on \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\).
nodes.formal:

addition and multiplication determine unique outputs.
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
For each positive integer \(n\), the representative formulas for modular
addition and multiplication determine unique outputs.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}
Suppose \(a\equiv a'\pmod n\) and \(b\equiv b'\pmod n\). Then
\(a-a'=nk\) and \(b-b'=n\ell\). Hence
\[
(a+b)-(a'+b')=n(k+\ell),
\]
so \(a+b\equiv a'+b'\pmod n\). Also
\[
ab-a'b'=b(a-a')+a'(b-b')=n(bk+a'\ell),
\]
so \(ab\equiv a'b'\pmod n\). Therefore the class formulas for addition and
multiplication do not depend on the chosen representatives.

The proof shows that integer addition and multiplication respect congruence
modulo \(n\).

Changing representatives does not change the output, so the operations
belong to \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) itself.

nodes.name: The Two-Element System Is a Field
nodes.question: State the theorem: The Two-Element System Is a Field.
nodes.statement_display: The two-element number system \(\mathbb{F}_2\) is a field.
nodes.statement_tex: The two-element number system \(\mathbb{F}_2\) is a field.
nodes.formal: The structure \(\mathbb{F}_2\) satisfies the field axioms.
nodes.fully_quantified_form: The structure \(\mathbb{F}_2\) satisfies the field axioms.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}
The operation tables show closure. Addition is associative and commutative by
checking the eight possible triples, \(0\) is the additive identity, and each
element is its own additive inverse. Multiplication is associative and
commutative by the same finite check, \(1\) is the multiplicative identity,
and the only nonzero element is \(1\), whose multiplicative inverse is \(1\).
The distributive law is verified on the eight possible triples. Hence the
field axioms hold.
nodes.proof_idea: Finite operation tables turn the field axioms into a finite verification.
nodes.source_text: The two tables make the smallest field visible by direct finite verification.
