nodes.name: The Two-Element System Is Not an Ordered Field
nodes.question: State the theorem: The Two-Element System Is Not an Ordered Field.
nodes.statement_display:
There is no order on \(\mathbb{B}_2\) that makes
\(\mathbb{F}_2\) an ordered field.
nodes.statement_tex:
There is no order on \(\mathbb{B}_2\) that makes
\(\mathbb{F}_2\) an ordered field.
nodes.formal: No order on \(\mathbb{B}_2\) makes \(\mathbb{F}_2\) satisfy the ordered-field axioms.
nodes.fully_quantified_form: No order on \(\mathbb{B}_2\) makes \(\mathbb{F}_2\) satisfy the ordered-field axioms.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}
In any ordered field, \(1>0\), and addition preserves strict order. Adding
\(1\) to both sides gives \(1+1>0+1\). In \(\mathbb{F}_2\), however,
\(1+1=0\) and \(0+1=1\), so this would imply \(0>1\), contradicting
\(1>0\). Thus no compatible field order exists.
nodes.proof_idea:
The obstruction is algebraic: the identity \(1+1=0\) is incompatible with
ordered-field positivity and additive order preservation.
nodes.source_text: The equation \(1+1=0\) is compatible with field arithmetic but incompatible with ordered-field arithmetic.
depends_on_titles: The Two-Element System Is a Field

nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\) has the same carrier size and operation tables as

nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
\textbf{Professional Standard Proof.}
Every integer is congruent modulo \(2\) to either \(0\) or \(1\), so the
quotient has classes \([0]_2\) and \([1]_2\). The modular operation formulas
give \([1]_2+[1]_2=[2]_2=[0]_2\), \([0]_2+[1]_2=[1]_2\), and
\([1]_2\cdot[1]_2=[1]_2\), with products by \([0]_2\) equal to \([0]_2\).
These are exactly the two operation tables defining \(\mathbb{F}_2\).
nodes.proof_idea: The quotient construction specializes to the explicit two-row tables.
nodes.source_text: The two-element table system is the first modular arithmetic system.

nodes.name: Structure-Preserving Map
nodes.question: State the definition: Structure-Preserving Map.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A$ and $B$ be ordered arithmetic systems with a specified common source
structure: selected constants, selected operations, and a strict order. A map
$\varphi:A\to B$ is \emph{structure-preserving} exactly when it preserves each
selected constant and, for every selected binary operation $\star$ and all
$a,a'\in A$,
\[
\varphi(a\star_A a')=\varphi(a)\star_B\varphi(a'),
\]
and $a<_A a' \Longrightarrow \varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a')$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $A$ and $B$ be ordered arithmetic systems with a specified common source
structure: selected constants, selected operations, and a strict order. A map
$\varphi:A\to B$ is \emph{structure-preserving} exactly when it preserves each
selected constant and, for every selected binary operation $\star$ and all
$a,a'\in A$,
\[
\varphi(a\star_A a')=\varphi(a)\star_B\varphi(a'),
\]
and $a<_A a' \Longrightarrow \varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a')$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\varphi:A\to B \text{ is structure-preserving}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(\text{every selected constant is preserved}\\
&\qquad\land\ \text{every selected operation is preserved}\\
&\qquad\land \forall a,a'\in A\;(a<_A a' \Rightarrow \varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a'))\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\varphi:A\to B \text{ is structure-preserving}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(\text{every selected constant is preserved}\\
&\qquad\land\ \text{every selected operation is preserved}\\
&\qquad\land \forall a,a'\in A\;(a<_A a' \Rightarrow \varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a'))\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text:
A structure-preserving map carries the chosen arithmetic and order from $A$
into $B$ without distortion. The choice of structure matters: the positive
part of $\mathbb{W}$ carries the Peano successor from $\mathbb{N}$, while
the later ring and field embeddings focus on $0$, $1$, addition,
multiplication, and order. A structure-preserving map need not be injective;
collapsing distinct elements is still allowed at this stage. Injectivity is
added separately to obtain an embedding.

nodes.failure_modes: An embedding can fail in three structurally distinct ways: it may collapse two distinct elements to the same image (injectivity fails), fail to transport one of the selected constants or operations (algebraic preservation fails), or fail to preserve or reflect a strict-order comparison (order embedding fails).
nodes.source_text:
Most embeddings after $\mathbb{W}$ transport the \emph{ordered ring/field}
structure: constants, the two operations, and order. The first bridge
$\mathbb{N}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{W}$ is slightly different because
$\mathbb{N}$ is one-based and carries Peano successor. That local theorem is
proved in the whole-number chapter. In every case, induction is not transported
to the larger target: the phrase ``the naturals sit inside the integers'' must
not be read as carrying induction across all of $\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.question: State the theorem: Embeddings Identify a System with Its Image.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\varphi:A\to B$ be an embedding of ordered arithmetic systems relative to
a selected source structure. Then the corestriction $\varphi:A\to\varphi(A)$
is an isomorphism onto its image: it is a bijection that preserves and reflects
the selected constants, operations, and order. Consequently $A$ may be
identified with the corresponding substructure $\varphi(A)\subseteq B$.
nodes.statement_tex:

identified with the corresponding substructure $\varphi(A)\subseteq B$.

nodes.name: Compatibility of the Embedding Chain
nodes.question: State the theorem: Compatibility of the Embedding Chain.
nodes.statement_display: Let $\iota_{1}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{W}$, $\iota_{2}:\mathbb{W}\to\mathbb{Z}$, $\iota_{3}:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$, and $\iota_{4}:\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{R}$ be the canonical embeddings. For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ the composite $(\iota_{4}\circ\iota_{3}\circ\iota_{2}\circ\iota_{1})(n)$ is the real number identified with $n$, and the composite preserves the arithmetic and order carried by the source system. Hence arithmetic computed in any system agrees with arithmetic on its image in $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $\iota_{1}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{W}$, $\iota_{2}:\mathbb{W}\to\mathbb{Z}$, $\iota_{3}:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$, and $\iota_{4}:\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{R}$ be the canonical embeddings. For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ the composite $(\iota_{4}\circ\iota_{3}\circ\iota_{2}\circ\iota_{1})(n)$ is the real number identified with $n$, and the composite preserves the arithmetic and order carried by the source system. Hence arithmetic computed in any system agrees with arithmetic on its image in $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\forall n,m\in\mathbb{N}\;\bigl(\Phi(n+m)=\Phi(n)+\Phi(m)\ \land\ \Phi(n\cdot m)=\Phi(n)\cdot\Phi(m)\ \land\ (n<m\Leftrightarrow\Phi(n)<\Phi(m))\bigr),\quad \Phi=\iota_{4}\circ\iota_{3}\circ\iota_{2}\circ\iota_{1}.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\forall n,m\in\mathbb{N}\;\bigl(\Phi(n+m)=\Phi(n)+\Phi(m)\ \land\ \Phi(n\cdot m)=\Phi(n)\cdot\Phi(m)\ \land\ (n<m\Leftrightarrow\Phi(n)<\Phi(m))\bigr),\quad \Phi=\iota_{4}\circ\iota_{3}\circ\iota_{2}\circ\iota_{1}.
\]
nodes.source_text: Compatibility is what makes the single symbol $2$ well-defined across the whole chain: the answer to $2+2$ is the same whether computed in $\mathbb{N}$ or after embedding into $\mathbb{R}$. Without this coherence the inclusion notation would silently carry two different meanings for the same numeral.

nodes.statement_display:
Two expressions $x$ and $y$ are \emph{identical} when they denote the same
object.

nodes.source_text:
Identity is sameness, not similarity. It is the relation used when no
distinction remains between two denotations.

nodes.name: Leibniz's Law
nodes.question: State the axiom: Leibniz's Law.
nodes.statement_display:
Identical objects have exactly the same properties.
\[
\forall x\,\forall y\,
\Bigl(x=y \Longrightarrow \forall P\,\bigl(P(x)\Longleftrightarrow P(y)\bigr)\Bigr).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Identical objects have exactly the same properties.
\[
\forall x\,\forall y\,
\Bigl(x=y \Longrightarrow \forall P\,\bigl(P(x)\Longleftrightarrow P(y)\bigr)\Bigr).
\]

\[
\operatorname{Indiscernible}(x,y)
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall P\,\bigl(P(x)\Longleftrightarrow P(y)\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[

\Longleftrightarrow

\]
nodes.source_text:
Leibniz's law says that equality permits no observable mathematical
difference. Any property true of one equal object is true of the other.

nodes.name: Equality on a Domain
nodes.question: State the definition: Equality on a Domain.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A$ be a domain. \emph{Equality on $A$} is the relation, written $=$,
that holds exactly when two terms or constructions denote the same element of
$A$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $A$ be a domain. \emph{Equality on $A$} is the relation, written $=$,
that holds exactly when two terms or constructions denote the same element of
$A$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\operatorname{Equality}_A(=)
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall x,y \in A,\,
\bigl(x=y \Longleftrightarrow x \text{ and } y \text{ denote the same element of } A\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\operatorname{Equality}_A(=)
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall x,y \in A,\,
\bigl(x=y \Longleftrightarrow x \text{ and } y \text{ denote the same element of } A\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text:
Equality is the identity relation restricted to the domain currently under
discussion. Later equivalence relations may identify objects for a purpose,
but equality records literal sameness.

nodes.name: Definitional and Propositional Equality
nodes.question: State the definition: Definitional and Propositional Equality.
nodes.statement_display:
\emph{Definitional equality} records an introduced meaning, written with
$:=$. \emph{Propositional equality} is a statement of sameness inside the
theory, written with $=$.
nodes.statement_tex:
\emph{Definitional equality} records an introduced meaning, written with

theory, written with $=$.
nodes.source_text:
The distinction prevents definitions from being confused with theorems.
Definitions create abbreviations; propositional equalities must be available
as axioms, assumptions, or proved statements.

nodes.name: Symmetry of Equality

nodes.statement_display:

\]

\[
\forall x\,\forall y,\ (x=y \Longrightarrow y=x).
\]

\[

nodes.name: Addition Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the theorem: Addition Is Well-Defined on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
f_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
f_m(1)=S(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(f_m(S(n))=S(f_m(n))).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m+n \coloneqq f_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
f_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
f_m(1)=S(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(f_m(S(n))=S(f_m(n))).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m+n \coloneqq f_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Fix $m\in P$. Since $(P,S,1)$ is a Peano system, $S:P\to P$ is a function.
By closure under successor, $S(m)\in P$. Thus $(P,S(m),S)$ is iterator data
for $(P,S,1)$. By the Peano Iterator Theorem, there exists a unique function
\[
f_m:P\to P
\]
such that
\[
f_m(1)=S(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f_m(S(n))=S(f_m(n))).
\]
This proves existence and uniqueness of the recursively specified function
for the fixed element $m$.

Since $m\in P$ was arbitrary, each $m\in P$ determines exactly one such
function $f_m$. Define
\[
+:P\times P\to P
\qquad\text{by}\qquad
(m,n)\longmapsto m+n\coloneqq f_m(n).
\]
For every pair $(m,n)\in P\times P$, the value $f_m(n)$ lies in $P$, because
$f_m:P\to P$. The uniqueness of each $f_m$ makes the value assigned to each
pair uniquely determined. Hence the displayed rule defines a unique binary
operation on $P$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof fixes the left input $m$ and packages the recursive data as the
iterator data $(P,S(m),S)$. Closure under successor supplies the initial value
$S(m)\in P$, and the Peano Iterator Theorem supplies the unique function
$f_m:P\to P$. Varying $m$ then defines the binary operation pointwise by
$m+n=f_m(n)$; uniqueness is pointwise uniqueness of the iterator functions.
nodes.source_text:
The theorem shows that the recursive clauses for addition determine exactly one
right-input map for each fixed left input. The addition operation is therefore
not assumed; it is constructed from the successor map by recursion.

nodes.name: Multiplication Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the theorem: Multiplication Is Well-Defined on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
g_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
g_m(1)=m
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(g_m(S(n))=g_m(n)+m).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m \cdot n \coloneqq g_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
g_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
g_m(1)=m
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(g_m(S(n))=g_m(n)+m).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m \cdot n \coloneqq g_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.
nodes.source_text:
The recursive clauses for multiplication determine exactly one right-input map
for each fixed left input. The multiplication operation is therefore
constructed from recursion and addition rather than assumed at the outset.

nodes.name: Right Cancellation for Multiplication
nodes.question: State the theorem: Right Cancellation for Multiplication.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,c \in P$,
\[
b\cdot a=c\cdot a
\Longrightarrow
b=c.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:

\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:

\]
nodes.source_text:
Right cancellation is the symmetric form of multiplicative cancellation. It
follows from left cancellation together with commutativity of multiplication.

nodes.name: Cancellation for Multiplication
nodes.question: State the theorem: Cancellation for Multiplication.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Multiplication on $P$ satisfies cancellation
on both sides:
\[
a\cdot b=a\cdot c\Longrightarrow b=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
b\cdot a=c\cdot a\Longrightarrow b=c.
\]

\]

nodes.name: Strict Less Than on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the definition: Strict Less Than on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $a,b \in P$. One writes
\[
a<b
\]
exactly when there exists $c \in P$ such that
\[
b=a+c.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $a,b \in P$. One writes
\[
a<b
\]
exactly when there exists $c \in P$ such that
\[
b=a+c.
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a<b
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists c \in P\;(b=a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a<b
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists c \in P\;(b=a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not< b
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall c \in P\;(b \neq a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not< b
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall c \in P\;(b \neq a+c).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
Strict inequality fails exactly when no additive witness in $P$ carries $a$ to
$b$. In that case, every nontrivial additive step from $a$ misses $b$.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not< b
\Longleftrightarrow
\underbrace{\forall c \in P\;(b \neq a+c)}_{\text{every proposed additive witness fails}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text:
The strict order records whether $b$ lies genuinely ahead of $a$ in the
counting structure. The witness $c$ is the amount of additive displacement
needed to move from $a$ to $b$.

nodes.name: Less Than or Equal on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the definition: Less Than or Equal on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $a,b \in P$. One writes
\[
a \le b
\]
exactly when
\[
a<b
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
a=b.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:

\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \le b
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(a<b \lor a=b\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[

\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not\le b
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(a \not< b \land a \neq b\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
&a \not\le b
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(a \not< b \land a \neq b\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
The non-strict order fails in exactly two simultaneous ways: $a$ is not
strictly below $b$, and $a$ is not equal to $b$. Thus $b$ neither lies ahead
of $a$ nor coincides with it.
nodes.source_text:
The relation $a \le b$ allows either equality or a genuine forward step from
$a$ to $b$. It is the additive order relation derived from the strict witness
definition.

nodes.name: Order Is Transitive on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the theorem: Order Is Transitive on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,c \in P$,
\[
\bigl(a \le b \land b \le c\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
a \le c.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,c \in P$,
\[
\bigl(a \le b \land b \le c\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
a \le c.
\]
nodes.source_text:
If $b$ lies at or beyond $a$, and $c$ lies at or beyond $b$, then $c$ also
lies at or beyond $a$. Transitivity expresses the consistency of additive
comparison along a chain.

nodes.name: Trichotomy on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the theorem: Trichotomy on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b \in P$, exactly one of the
following holds:
\[
a<b,\qquad a=b,\qquad b<a.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b \in P$, exactly one of the
following holds:
\[
a<b,\qquad a=b,\qquad b<a.
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system.}\\
&\forall a,b \in P\;
\Bigl(
(a<b \lor a=b \lor b<a) \land {}\\
&\qquad\neg(a<b \land a=b) \land
\neg(a<b \land b<a) \land
\neg(a=b \land b<a)
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system.}\\
&\forall a,b \in P\;
\Bigl(
(a<b \lor a=b \lor b<a) \land {}\\
&\qquad\neg(a<b \land a=b) \land
\neg(a<b \land b<a) \land
\neg(a=b \land b<a)
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text:
Any two elements of a Peano system are linearly comparable: one lies below the
other, or they coincide. Trichotomy is the theorem that upgrades the additive
comparison relation from a partial-order structure to a total order.

nodes.name: Exponentiation on a Peano System
nodes.question: State the definition: Exponentiation on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For each $a \in P$, define the function
\[
h_a : P \to P
\]
to be the unique function satisfying
\[
h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).
\]
For $a,n \in P$, define
\[
a^n \coloneqq h_a(n).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For each $a \in P$, define the function
\[
h_a : P \to P
\]
to be the unique function satisfying
\[
h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).
\]
For $a,n \in P$, define
\[
a^n \coloneqq h_a(n).
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system. For each } a \in P,
\text{ let } h_a : P \to P \text{ satisfy}\\
&h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).\\
&\text{Then for all } a,n \in P,\quad a^n \coloneqq h_a(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system. For each } a \in P,
\text{ let } h_a : P \to P \text{ satisfy}\\
&h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).\\
&\text{Then for all } a,n \in P,\quad a^n \coloneqq h_a(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system. For each } a \in P,
\text{ let } h_a : P \to P \text{ satisfy}\\
&h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).\\
&\text{Then for all } a,n,x \in P,\quad
x \neq a^n \Longleftrightarrow x \neq h_a(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system. For each } a \in P,
\text{ let } h_a : P \to P \text{ satisfy}\\
&h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).\\
&\text{Then for all } a,n,x \in P,\quad
x \neq a^n \Longleftrightarrow x \neq h_a(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text:
Exponentiation is repeated multiplication in the same sense that multiplication
is repeated addition. The base $a$ is the fixed left factor; the exponent $n$
counts how many times $a$ is multiplied together. The recursive definition
propagates rightward: $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a^1 \cdot a = a \cdot a$, and so on.

nodes.question: State the theorem: Exponentiation Is Well-Defined on a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
h_a:P\to P
\]
such that
\[
h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(a,n)\longmapsto a^n\coloneqq h_a(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

nodes.question: State the theorem: $n < 2^n$ for All $n $.
nodes.statement_display:

\[
n < 2^n.

nodes.source_text:
The base case $1 < 2 = 2^1$ holds by definition of $2$ and the strict order.
For the inductive step, assume $n < 2^n$. Then $2^{S(n)} = 2^n \cdot 2$.
Since $2^n > n \ge 1$, we have $2^n \cdot 2 > n \cdot 2 = n + n > n + 1 = S(n)$,
where the last step uses that $n \ge 1$ so $n + n > n + 1$. Hence $S(n) < 2^{S(n)}$.
The inequality $n < 2^n$ is the threshold that distinguishes the growth regimes
and reappears in every comparison between polynomial and exponential bounds.

nodes.name: Well-Ordering Principle
nodes.question: State the theorem: Well-Ordering Principle.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
element with respect to the order $\le$ on $P$.
nodes.statement_tex:

nodes.failure_modes:
The well-ordering principle would fail if some nonempty subset of $P$ had no
least element. That means for every candidate minimum, a strictly smaller
element of the subset exists, producing an infinite strictly descending chain
in $P$. Induction rules this out.
nodes.source_text:
The well-ordering principle is the order-theoretic complement to induction.
Induction says one can build up: start at $1$ and keep stepping forward.
Well-ordering says one can always descend to a minimum: any nonempty set has
a floor. Proof strategies that use well-ordering typically assume a property
fails somewhere, form the set of failures, extract its minimum by
well-ordering, and derive a contradiction from the minimality of that element.

nodes.name: Induction, Strong Induction, and Well-Ordering Are Equivalent
nodes.question: State the theorem: Induction, Strong Induction, and Well-Ordering Are Equivalent.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system equipped with the order $\le$. The following
are equivalent:
- The induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$, if
 $\varphi(1)$ holds and the successor step holds, then $\varphi(n)$ holds
 for all $n \in P$.
- The strong induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$,
 if $\varphi(k)$ holds for every $k<n$ implies $\varphi(n)$, then
 $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$.
- The well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
 element with respect to $\le$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system equipped with the order $\le$. The following
are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item The induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$, if
 $\varphi(1)$ holds and the successor step holds, then $\varphi(n)$ holds
 for all $n \in P$.
 \item The strong induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$,
 if $\varphi(k)$ holds for every $k<n$ implies $\varphi(n)$, then
 $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$.
 \item The well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
 element with respect to $\le$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.source_text:
Induction proves well-ordering by contrapositive: if a nonempty set $A$ had
no least element, the set of non-members of $A$ would be inductive, forcing
$A = \varnothing$, a contradiction. Well-ordering proves induction by forming
the set of elements where $\varphi$ fails and, if nonempty, extracting a
least failure to derive a contradiction with the successor step.

nodes.name: $ $ Is Closed, Associative, and Commutative Under Addition
nodes.question: State the theorem: $ $ Is Closed, Associative, and Commutative Under Addition.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $+$ on $P$ satisfies:
- \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b \in P$.
- \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$.
- \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b = b+a$.
- \textbf{Left cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $a+b = a+c$ then $b=c$.
- \textbf{Right cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $b+a = c+a$ then $b=c$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $+$ on $P$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b \in P$.
 \item \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$.
 \item \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b = b+a$.
 \item \textbf{Left cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $a+b = a+c$ then $b=c$.
 \item \textbf{Right cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $b+a = c+a$ then $b=c$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.source_text:
This theorem is a packaging result. It names the algebraic structure that
has been proved piece by piece: the three individual theorems on associativity,
commutativity, and cancellation together certify that $(P,+)$ is a cancellative
commutative semigroup. There is no additive identity in $P$ because $P$ has
no element $0$ with $0+n=n$ for all $n$; the smallest element under addition
is $1$, not an identity.

nodes.name: $ $ Is a Commutative Monoid Under Multiplication
nodes.question: State the theorem: $ $ Is a Commutative Monoid Under Multiplication.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $\cdot$ on $P$ satisfies:
- \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a \cdot b \in P$.
- \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.
- \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$,
 $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$.
- \textbf{Identity.} For all $a \in P$,
 $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$.
Consequently $(P, \cdot, 1)$ is a commutative monoid.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $\cdot$ on $P$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a \cdot b \in P$.
 \item \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
 $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.
 \item \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$,
 $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$.
 \item \textbf{Identity.} For all $a \in P$,
 $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $(P, \cdot, 1)$ is a commutative monoid.
nodes.source_text:
The distinguished first element $1$ is a multiplicative identity on both
sides, so multiplication promotes $P$ from a semigroup to a monoid. The
absence of multiplicative inverses (other than $1^{-1} = 1$, which does not
lie in $P$ in the usual sense) is what prevents $(P,\cdot)$ from being a
group. The structural limitation is intrinsic: no element of $P$ other than
$1$ has a reciprocal in $P$.

\begin{enumerate}
 \item $(P,+)$ is a commutative semigroup.

 \item Multiplication distributes over addition: for all $a,b,c \in P$,

nodes.source_text:
A semiring packages the interaction of two operations without requiring
additive inverses. The natural numbers are the canonical example of a semiring
that is not a ring: they satisfy every ring axiom except the existence of
additive inverses, which fails because there is no element $-1$ in $P$.
The integers are the smallest ring extending $P$ that repairs this failure.

nodes.name: Peano System
nodes.question: State the definition: Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
A triple $(P,S,1)$ is called a \emph{Peano system} exactly when $P$ is a set,
$1 \in P$, $S : P \to P$ is a function, and the following axioms hold:
- $1 \in P$.
- For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \in P$.
- For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \neq 1$.
- For all $m,n \in P$, if $S(m)=S(n)$ then $m=n$.
- If $A \subseteq P$, $1 \in A$, and
 \[
 \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A),
 \]
 then $A=P$.
nodes.statement_tex:
A triple $(P,S,1)$ is called a \emph{Peano system} exactly when $P$ is a set,
$1 \in P$, $S : P \to P$ is a function, and the following axioms hold:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item[\textbf{P1.}] $1 \in P$.
 \item[\textbf{P2.}] For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \in P$.
 \item[\textbf{P3.}] For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \neq 1$.
 \item[\textbf{P4.}] For all $m,n \in P$, if $S(m)=S(n)$ then $m=n$.
 \item[\textbf{P5.}] If $A \subseteq P$, $1 \in A$, and
 \[
 \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A),
 \]
 then $A=P$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(P,S,1) \text{ is a Peano system}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(P \text{ is a set} \land 1 \in P \land S : P \to P \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \in P) \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \neq 1) \\
&\qquad \land \forall m,n \in P\;(S(m)=S(n) \Longrightarrow m=n) \\
&\qquad \land \forall A \subseteq P\;
\bigl((1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A))
\Longrightarrow A=P\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(P,S,1) \text{ is a Peano system}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(P \text{ is a set} \land 1 \in P \land S : P \to P \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \in P) \\

&\qquad \land \forall m,n \in P\;(S(m)=S(n) \Longrightarrow m=n) \\
&\qquad \land \forall A \subseteq P\;
\bigl((1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A))
\Longrightarrow A=P\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes:
A triple $(P,S,1)$ fails to be a Peano system if the distinguished element
does not lie in the underlying set, if the successor map leaves the set, if
the successor hits $1$, if the successor identifies two distinct elements, or
if there exists a proper subset of $P$ that contains $1$ and is closed under
successor.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\neg\,\text{$(P,S,1)$ is a Peano system}
\Longrightarrow\;&
1 \notin P \\
&\lor \exists n \in P\;(S(n) \notin P) \\
&\lor \exists n \in P\;(S(n)=1) \\
&\lor \exists m,n \in P\;(m \neq n \land S(m)=S(n)) \\
&\lor \exists A \subseteq P\;
\bigl(1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A)
\land A \neq P\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.source_text:
A Peano system is the abstract data of counting: an underlying set, a first
element, and a successor operation satisfying the usual non-collision and
induction principles. The purpose of the definition is to isolate the ambient
object before the individual axioms are recorded and used one by one.

nodes.name: Induction Principle for a Peano System
nodes.question: State the theorem: Induction Principle for a Peano System.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$.
If
\[
\varphi(1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n))),
\]
then
\[
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$.
If
\[
\varphi(1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n))),
\]
then
\[
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Define $A \coloneqq \{\,n \in P \mid \varphi(n)\,\}$.
The hypothesis $\varphi(1)$ gives $1 \in A$.
The hypothesis $\forall n \in P\,(\varphi(n) \Rightarrow \varphi(S(n)))$
gives $\forall n \in P\,(n \in A \Rightarrow S(n) \in A)$.
Hence $A$ is an inductive subset of $P$.
By the induction axiom \hyperref[ax:peano-induction]{(P5)}, $A = P$.
Therefore $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof is a direct application of the induction axiom (P5). The induction
axiom is formulated in terms of subsets: any inductive subset of $P$ must
equal $P$ itself. The predicate $\varphi$ does not appear in (P5), so the
first move is always to translate --- passing from the predicate form to the
subset form via the extension $A \coloneqq \{\,n \in P \mid \varphi(n)\,\}$.
Once the translation is made, the two hypotheses map exactly onto the two
conditions that (P5) requires: the base condition $1 \in A$ comes from
$\varphi(1)$, and successor-closure of $A$ comes from the step hypothesis on
$\varphi$. The induction axiom then forces $A = P$, and translating back gives
the conclusion.

This translation pattern --- predicate to subset, apply (P5), translate back
--- is the invariant structure of every induction proof in the Peano system
framework.

nodes.name: Every Element Is Either $1$ or a Successor
nodes.question: State the theorem: Every Element Is Either $1$ or a Successor.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, either $x=1$ or there
exists $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $x \in P$, either $x=1$ or there
exists $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let
\[
D:=\{x\in P:x=1 \text{ or } \exists u\in P\;(S(u)=x)\}.
\]
We show that $D$ is inductive. Since $1=1$, we have $1\in D$.

Now let $x\in D$. By closure of successor, $S(x)\in P$. Moreover $x\in P$,
so $S(x)$ is the successor of an element of $P$. Hence $S(x)\in D$.
Therefore $D$ contains $1$ and is closed under successor. By the induction
principle, $D=P$.

Thus every $x\in P$ lies in $D$, so every $x\in P$ satisfies either $x=1$ or
there exists $u\in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof forms the subset of all elements satisfying the desired dichotomy
and then proves that this subset is inductive. The base case is immediate
from $1=1$. The successor step is immediate because every successor is, by
definition, a successor of an element of $P$.

nodes.name: Predecessor Existence and Uniqueness Away from $1$
nodes.question: State the corollary: Predecessor Existence and Uniqueness Away from $1$.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $x \in P$ with $x \neq 1$. Then
there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $x \in P$ with $x \neq 1$. Then
there exists a unique $u \in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
By
\hyperref[thm:every-element-is-one-or-a-successor]{Every Element Is Either
$1$ or a Successor}, either $x=1$ or there exists $u\in P$ such that
$S(u)=x$. Since $x\neq 1$, the first alternative is impossible. Hence there
exists $u\in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.

To prove uniqueness, let $v\in P$ and suppose $S(v)=x$. Since also $S(u)=x$,
we have
\[
S(v)=S(u).
\]
By injectivity of the successor map, $v=u$. Therefore there exists a unique
$u\in P$ such that $S(u)=x$.
nodes.proof_idea:
Existence comes from the dichotomy theorem after ruling out the case $x=1$.
Uniqueness is a direct application of injectivity of the successor map: two
elements with the same successor must be equal.
nodes.source_text:
Every element distinct from $1$ has exactly one predecessor. The successor map
therefore organizes the non-initial part of a Peano system into one-step
extensions of earlier elements.

nodes.name: The Distinguished Element Is the Unique Non-Successor
nodes.question: State the corollary: The Distinguished Element Is the Unique Non-Successor.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. An element $x \in P$ is not a successor of
any element of $P$ if and only if $x=1$.
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. An element $x \in P$ is not a successor of
any element of $P$ if and only if $x=1$.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Assume first that $x\in P$ is not a successor of any element of $P$. By
\hyperref[thm:every-element-is-one-or-a-successor]{Every Element Is Either
$1$ or a Successor}, either $x=1$ or there exists $u\in P$ such that
$S(u)=x$. The second alternative contradicts the assumption that $x$ is not a
successor. Hence $x=1$.

Conversely, suppose $x=1$. By the Peano axiom that $1$ is not a successor,
there is no $u\in P$ such that $S(u)=1$. Since $x=1$, there is no $u\in P$
such that $S(u)=x$. Therefore $x$ is not a successor of any element of $P$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The forward implication uses the dichotomy theorem and eliminates the
successor case. The reverse implication is exactly the Peano axiom that the
distinguished element is not a successor.
nodes.source_text:
The distinguished first element is characterized internally as the unique
element with no predecessor. This gives a structural description of $1$ that
does not depend on external notation.
depends_on_titles: Distinguished Element Is Not a Successor
Predecessor Existence and Uniqueness Away from $1$

nodes.name: No Object Is Its Own Successor
nodes.question: State the theorem: No Object Is Its Own Successor.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $n \in P$,
\[
S(n) \neq n.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $n \in P$,
\[
S(n) \neq n.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let
\[
D:=\{x\in P:S(x)\neq x\}.
\]
We prove that $D=P$ by induction.

First, $1\in D$. Indeed, if $S(1)=1$, then $1$ would be the successor of the
element $1\in P$, contradicting the Peano axiom that $1$ is not a successor.
Thus $S(1)\neq 1$.

Now assume $n\in D$. Then $S(n)\neq n$. If $S(S(n))=S(n)$, injectivity of
$S$ would imply $S(n)=n$, contradicting $n\in D$. Therefore
$S(S(n))\neq S(n)$, so $S(n)\in D$.

Thus $D$ contains $1$ and is closed under successor. By the induction
principle, $D=P$. Hence for every $n\in P$, $S(n)\neq n$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof uses induction on the subset of elements that are not equal to
their own successors. The base case uses the axiom that $1$ is not a
successor. The successor step uses the contrapositive form of injectivity:
from $S(n)\neq n$, one obtains $S(S(n))\neq S(n)$.

nodes.name: Consistency of the Minimal Iterator Relation
nodes.question: State the lemma: Consistency of the Minimal Iterator Relation.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
$R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation for $(W,c,g)$. Then $R^*$ is an
iterator relation for $(W,c,g)$.

Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
$R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation for $(W,c,g)$. Then $R^*$ is an
iterator relation for $(W,c,g)$.
nodes.formal:
\[
R^* \text{ is an iterator relation for } (W,c,g).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
R^* \text{ is an iterator relation for } (W,c,g).
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
R^* \text{ is not an iterator relation for } (W,c,g).
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
R^* \text{ is not an iterator relation for } (W,c,g).
\]
nodes.contrapositive:
\[

\Longrightarrow
R^* \text{ is not the minimal iterator relation for } (W,c,g).
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let
\[
\mathcal R=
\{R\subseteq P\times W : R \text{ is an iterator relation for } (W,c,g)\}.
\]
By definition,
\[
R^*=\bigcap \mathcal R.
\]
We verify the three clauses in the definition of an iterator relation.

First, since every member of $\mathcal R$ is a subset of $P\times W$, its
intersection is also a subset of $P\times W$. Hence
\[
R^*\subseteq P\times W.
\]

Second, let $R\in\mathcal R$. Because $R$ is an iterator relation,
$(1,c)\in R$. Since this holds for every $R\in\mathcal R$, the pair $(1,c)$
belongs to the intersection. Thus
\[
(1,c)\in R^*.
\]

Third, suppose $n\in P$, $w\in W$, and $(n,w)\in R^*$. Let $R\in\mathcal R$.
Then $(n,w)\in R$, because $R^*$ is the intersection of all relations in
\(\mathcal R\). Since $R$ is an iterator relation, it is closed under the
iterator step, so
\[
(S(n),g(w))\in R.
\]
This holds for every $R\in\mathcal R$, and therefore
\[
(S(n),g(w))\in R^*.
\]

We have shown that $R^*\subseteq P\times W$, that $(1,c)\in R^*$, and that
$R^*$ is closed under the iterator step. Hence $R^*$ is an iterator relation
for $(W,c,g)$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof uses the closure properties that define the class of iterator
relations and verifies that those properties are preserved by intersection.
The base-pair and step-closure clauses hold in every iterator relation in the
family, so they hold in the intersection that defines $R^*$. The argument is
therefore a direct verification from the definition of the minimal iterator
relation.
nodes.source_text:
The intersection construction does not lose the base pair or the successor
closure condition. The minimal relation is therefore still one of the
admissible iterator relations.

nodes.question: State the lemma: Uniqueness of Iterator Functions.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it. If
$f,h:P\to W$ satisfy
\[
f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n))),
\]
then $f=h$.
nodes.statement_tex:

\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n))),
\]

\Longrightarrow f=h\Bigr).

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Binary Iterator Operations
nodes.question: State the corollary: Uniqueness of Binary Iterator Operations.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $A$ be a set, let $W$ be a set, and
suppose each $a\in A$ determines iterator data $(W,c_a,g_a)$ for $(P,S,1)$.
If $F,G:A\times P\to W$ satisfy
\[
F(a,1)=c_a,\qquad G(a,1)=c_a
\]
and
\[
F(a,S(n))=g_a(F(a,n)),
\qquad
G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))
\]
for all $a\in A$ and all $n\in P$, then $F=G$.

If $F,G:A\times P\to W$ satisfy

F(a,1)=c_a,\qquad G(a,1)=c_a
\]

\[

\qquad
G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))
\]
for all $a\in A$ and all $n\in P$, then $F=G$.

\]

\Longrightarrow F=G.

nodes.name: General Recursive Function
nodes.question: State the definition: General Recursive Function.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $W$ be a set, let $c\in W$, and let
$\Phi:P\times W\to W$ be a stage-dependent step rule. A function $f:P\to W$
is called the \emph{general recursive function determined by $(W,c,\Phi)$}
exactly when
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=\Phi(n,f(n))).
\]

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Peano Systems up to Isomorphism
nodes.question: State the theorem: Uniqueness of Peano Systems up to Isomorphism.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S_P,1_P)$ and $(Q,S_Q,1_Q)$ be Peano systems. Then there exists a
unique bijection $\theta:P\to Q$ such that
\[
\theta(1_P)=1_Q
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(\theta(S_P(n))=S_Q(\theta(n))).
\]
Thus any two Peano systems are isomorphic.

nodes.statement_display: The map $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ satisfies, for all $x,y,z\in\mathbb{R}$: (i) $d(x,y)\ge 0$ with $d(x,y)=0$ iff $x=y$; (ii) $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$; and (iii) $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Hence $(\mathbb{R},d)$ is a metric space.

\]

nodes.question: State the theorem: Closure Laws for Closed Sets.
nodes.statement_display: An arbitrary intersection of closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed, and a finite union of closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed.
nodes.statement_tex: An arbitrary intersection of closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed, and a finite union of closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ is closed.
nodes.formal:
\[
\Bigl(\forall i\in I\;F_i\text{ closed}\Bigr)\Longrightarrow \Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in I} F_{i}\Bigr) \text{ closed};\qquad
\Bigl(\bigwedge_{k=1}^{n} F_k\text{ closed}\Bigr)\Longrightarrow \Bigl(\bigcup_{k=1}^{n} F_{k}\Bigr) \text{ closed}.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\Bigl(\forall i\in I\;F_i\text{ closed}\Bigr)\Longrightarrow \Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in I} F_{i}\Bigr) \text{ closed};\qquad

nodes.statement_display: Let $\{U_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $E$. A \emph{subcover} is a subfamily $\{U_{i}\}_{i\in J}$ with $J\subseteq I$ that still covers $E$. It is a \emph{finite subcover} when $J$ is finite.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $\{U_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ be an open cover of $E$. A \emph{subcover} is a subfamily $\{U_{i}\}_{i\in J}$ with $J\subseteq I$ that still covers $E$. It is a \emph{finite subcover} when $J$ is finite.
nodes.formal:
\[
\{U_i\}_{i\in J} \text{ is a finite subcover of } E
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(J\subseteq I \land J \text{ is finite} \land E\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{i\in J}U_i\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\{U_i\}_{i\in J} \text{ is a finite subcover of } E
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(J\subseteq I \land J \text{ is finite} \land E\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{i\in J}U_i\bigr).
\]
nodes.source_text: A subcover discards some pieces while still covering $E$; a finite subcover discards all but finitely many. The existence of a finite subcover for \emph{every} open cover is the defining property of compactness.

nodes.question: State the definition: Compact Set in $ $.
nodes.statement_display:
A set $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is \emph{compact} exactly when every open cover of $K$ admits a finite subcover:
\[
\forall \{U_i\}_{i\in I}\text{ open cover of }K\;\exists \text{finite } J\subseteq I\;\Bigl(K\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in J}U_i\Bigr).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
A set $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is \emph{compact} exactly when every open cover of $K$ admits a finite subcover:
\[
\forall \{U_i\}_{i\in I}\text{ open cover of }K\;\exists \text{finite } J\subseteq I\;\Bigl(K\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in J}U_i\Bigr).
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
K \text{ compact} \Longleftrightarrow \forall \{U_i\}_{i\in I}\Bigl(\bigl(\forall i\in I\;U_i \text{ open}\bigr)\land K\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i \Rightarrow \exists \text{finite } J\subseteq I\;K\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{i\in J}U_i\Bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
K \text{ compact} \Longleftrightarrow \forall \{U_i\}_{i\in I}\Bigl(\bigl(\forall i\in I\;U_i \text{ open}\bigr)\land K\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i \Rightarrow \exists \text{finite } J\subseteq I\;K\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{i\in J}U_i\Bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
K \text{ not compact} \Longleftrightarrow \exists \{U_i\}_{i\in I}\Bigl(\bigl(\forall i\in I\;U_i \text{ open}\bigr)\land K\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i \land \forall \text{finite } J\subseteq I\;K\not\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{i\in J}U_i\Bigr).
\]

\[
K \text{ not compact} \Longleftrightarrow \exists \{U_i\}_{i\in I}\Bigl(\bigl(\forall i\in I\;U_i \text{ open}\bigr)\land K\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i \land \forall \text{finite } J\subseteq I\;K\not\subseteq\textstyle\bigcup_{i\in J}U_i\Bigr).

This is what later guarantees, on a compact domain, that continuous functions attain extrema and are uniformly continuous --- the facts Analysis~I relies on. nodes.question: State the definition: Least Upper Bound Property.
nodes.statement_display: Let $(S,\le)$ be an ordered set. The set $S$ has the \emph{Least Upper Bound Property} if and only if every nonempty subset of $S$ that is bounded above in $S$ has a supremum in $S$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $(S,\le)$ be an ordered set. The set $S$ has the \emph{Least Upper Bound Property} if and only if every nonempty subset of $S$ that is bounded above in $S$ has a supremum in $S$.
nodes.proposition:
\[
\operatorname{LeastUpperBoundProperty}(S)\coloneqq
\forall A\subseteq S\;
\Bigl[
\bigl(A\neq\varnothing \land \exists u\in S\;\forall x\in A\;(x\le u)\bigr)
\rightarrow
\exists s\in S\;\operatorname{Supremum}(s,A)
\Bigr].
\]

\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.failure_modes: The property fails when there is a nonempty subset of the ambient ordered set that has at least one upper bound but has no least upper bound inside that same ambient set.
nodes.source_text: The Least Upper Bound Property says that upper-bounded nonempty subsets do not point toward missing ceiling elements. Whenever the order supplies at least one upper bound, it also supplies a smallest upper bound in the same ambient set. Failure therefore indicates a hole in the ordered structure rather than a defect in the subset alone.

nodes.source_text: The completeness axiom asserts that the real line has no order gaps of the least-upper-bound kind. Nonempty sets of real numbers that are bounded above always determine a real number sitting exactly at the least possible ceiling. In Volume II, $\mathbb{R}$ is constructed as the complete ordered field arising from Dedekind cuts; in this volume, completeness is used as the standing least-upper-bound principle for real analysis. This is the structural property that distinguishes $\mathbb{R}$ from ordered fields such as $\mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.name: Nested Interval Property
nodes.question: State the theorem: Nested Interval Property.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(I_n)$ be a sequence of nonempty closed intervals in $\mathbb{R}$. If $I_{n+1}\subseteq I_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, then
\[
 \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} I_n\neq\varnothing.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $(I_n)$ be a sequence of nonempty closed intervals in $\mathbb{R}$. If $I_{n+1}\subseteq I_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, then
\[
 \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} I_n\neq\varnothing.
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall (a_n)\subseteq\mathbb{R}\;\forall (b_n)\subseteq\mathbb{R}\;\\
&\Bigl[
\bigl(\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(a_n\le b_n)\bigr)
\land
\bigl(\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;([a_{n+1},b_{n+1}]\subseteq [a_n,b_n])\bigr)
\\
&\qquad\rightarrow
\exists x\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(x\in [a_n,b_n])
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

\[

\]

\\
&\qquad\land
\forall x\in\mathbb{R}\;\exists n\in\mathbb{N}\;(x\notin [a_n,b_n])
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

\\

\Bigr].
\end{aligned}

nodes.failure_modes: The theorem fails when a nested sequence of nonempty closed real intervals has no common real point.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Since $I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n$, the sequence of endpoints satisfies $a_n \le a_{n+1} \le b_{n+1} \le b_n$. Thus, $(a_n)$ is monotone increasing and bounded above by $b_1$. By the Monotone Convergence Theorem, $a_n \to x$ where $x = \sup \{a_n\}$. For any fixed $k$, $a_n \le b_k$ for all $n$ (since if $n > k$, $a_n \le b_n \le b_k$, and if $n \le k$, $a_n \le a_k \le b_k$). Thus, $x = \sup \{a_n\} \le b_k$ for all $k$. Since $a_k \le x$ for all $k$, we have $a_k \le x \le b_k$, implying $x \in I_k$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Thus $x \in \bigcap I_n$.
nodes.proof_idea: The proof utilizes the Monotone Convergence/Least Upper Bound property to identify the supremum of the left endpoints as a point that is caught between the "rising floor" and the "falling ceiling" of the intervals.
nodes.source_text: Nested closed intervals cannot keep shrinking or relocating in a way that loses every real point. Nesting keeps the intervals aligned, nonemptiness prevents trivial collapse at each stage, and completeness supplies a real point that survives all stages at once.

nodes.name: Archimedean Property
nodes.question: State the theorem: Archimedean Property.
nodes.statement_display: For every real number $x$, there exists a natural number $n$ such that $n>x$.
nodes.statement_tex: For every real number $x$, there exists a natural number $n$ such that $n>x$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\forall x\in\mathbb{R}\;\exists n\in\mathbb{N}\;(n>x).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\forall x\in\mathbb{R}\;\exists n\in\mathbb{N}\;(n>x).
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\exists x\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(n\le x).
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\exists x\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(n\le x).
\]
nodes.failure_modes: The theorem fails exactly when the natural numbers are bounded above by some real number.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\neg\operatorname{ArchimedeanProperty}(\mathbb{R})
=
\underbrace{\exists x\in\mathbb{R}}_{\text{real upper bound}}
\;\underbrace{\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(n\le x)}_{\text{all natural numbers remain below it}}.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Assume for sake of contradiction that the property is false. Then there exists $x \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $n \le x$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This implies $\mathbb{N}$ is bounded above. By the Least Upper Bound Property of $\mathbb{R}$, $s = \sup \mathbb{N}$ exists. Since $s$ is the least upper bound, $s-1$ is not an upper bound. Thus, there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $m > s-1$, which implies $m+1 > s$. Since $m+1 \in \mathbb{N}$, this contradicts that $s$ is an upper bound for $\mathbb{N}$. Hence, $\mathbb{N}$ is unbounded.
nodes.proof_idea: The proof utilizes a contradiction strategy based on the completeness of the real numbers. It shows that if $\mathbb{N}$ were bounded, its "ceiling" would have to be surpassable by simply adding $1$ to a value near that ceiling.
nodes.source_text: The Archimedean Property says that the natural numbers do not stop below any real ceiling. No real number is so large that every natural number remains below it. In this chapter, the result is a consequence of completeness: a bounded copy of $\mathbb{N}$ would have a supremum, and that supremum is contradicted by shifting one natural number upward.

nodes.name: Archimedean Reciprocal Corollary
nodes.question: State the corollary: Archimedean Reciprocal Corollary.
nodes.statement_display: For every $x>0$ and every $y\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $nx>y$.
nodes.statement_tex: For every $x>0$ and every $y\in\mathbb{R}$, there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $nx>y$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}\;\bigl(x>0\rightarrow \exists n\in\mathbb{N}\;(nx>y)\bigr).
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}\;\bigl(x>0\rightarrow \exists n\in\mathbb{N}\;(nx>y)\bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\exists x,y\in\mathbb{R}\;\bigl(x>0\land \forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(nx\le y)\bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\exists x,y\in\mathbb{R}\;\bigl(x>0\land \forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(nx\le y)\bigr).
\]
nodes.failure_modes: The corollary fails when a positive real step size has all of its natural multiples bounded above by some real threshold.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\neg\operatorname{ArchimedeanReciprocal}(\mathbb{R})
=
\underbrace{\exists x\in\mathbb{R}\;(x>0)}_{\text{positive step size}}
\;\land\;
\underbrace{\exists y\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\;(nx\le y)}_{\text{all natural multiples stay bounded}}.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}$, its reciprocal $\frac{1}{\varepsilon}$ is also a real number. By the Archimedean Property, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n > \frac{1}{\varepsilon}$. Since $n$ and $\varepsilon$ are both positive, we can invert the inequality to obtain $\frac{1}{n} < \varepsilon$.
nodes.proof_idea: This is a direct proof utilizing the Archimedean Property of $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.source_text: Any fixed positive real step eventually passes any real threshold when repeated enough times. The statement is the Archimedean Property applied after rescaling by the positive number $x$: growth by units becomes growth by steps of size $x$.

nodes.name: Dense Subset
nodes.question: State the definition: Dense Subset.
nodes.statement_display: Let $D\subseteq S\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. The set $D$ is \emph{dense in} $S$ if and only if for every $x\in S$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $d\in D$ such that $|x-d|<\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $D\subseteq S\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. The set $D$ is \emph{dense in} $S$ if and only if for every $x\in S$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $d\in D$ such that $|x-d|<\varepsilon$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }D\subseteq S\subseteq\mathbb{R}.\\
&D\text{ is dense in }S
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall x\in S\;\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists d\in D\;\bigl(|x-d|<\varepsilon\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }D\subseteq S\subseteq\mathbb{R}.\\
&D\text{ is dense in }S
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall x\in S\;\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists d\in D\;\bigl(|x-d|<\varepsilon\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }D\subseteq S\subseteq\mathbb{R}.\\
&D\text{ is not dense in }S
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists x\in S\;\exists \varepsilon_0>0\;\forall d\in D\;\bigl(|x-d|\ge \varepsilon_0\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }D\subseteq S\subseteq\mathbb{R}.\\
&D\text{ is not dense in }S
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists x\in S\;\exists \varepsilon_0>0\;\forall d\in D\;\bigl(|x-d|\ge \varepsilon_0\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.failure_modes: Density fails when some point of $S$ has a positive-radius neighborhood that contains no point of $D$.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\neg\operatorname{DenseSubset}(D,S)
=
\underbrace{\exists x\in S}_{\text{point not approximated}}
\;\underbrace{\exists \varepsilon_0>0}_{\text{positive exclusion radius}}
\;\underbrace{\forall d\in D\;\bigl(|x-d|\ge \varepsilon_0\bigr)}_{\text{no point of }D\text{ enters the neighborhood}}.
\]
nodes.source_text: Density is an approximation property inside $S$. It does not say that every point of $S$ already belongs to $D$; it says that points of $D$ occur arbitrarily close to every point of $S$. Thus $D$ can be a proper subset of $S$ while still leaving no positive-width gap inside $S$.

nodes.name: Order Dense Subset
nodes.question: State the definition: Order Dense Subset.
nodes.statement_display: Let $X$ be a linearly ordered set and let $A\subseteq X$. The subset $A$ is \emph{order dense in} $X$ if and only if for every $a,b\in X$ with $a<b$ there exists $c\in A$ such that $a<c<b$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $X$ be a linearly ordered set and let $A\subseteq X$. The subset $A$ is \emph{order dense in} $X$ if and only if for every $a,b\in X$ with $a<b$ there exists $c\in A$ such that $a<c<b$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }X\text{ be a linearly ordered set and }A\subseteq X.\\
&A\text{ is order dense in }X
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall a,b\in X\;\bigl(a<b\rightarrow \exists c\in A\;(a<c<b)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }X\text{ be a linearly ordered set and }A\subseteq X.\\
&A\text{ is order dense in }X
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall a,b\in X\;\bigl(a<b\rightarrow \exists c\in A\;(a<c<b)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }X\text{ be a linearly ordered set and }A\subseteq X.\\
&A\text{ is not order dense in }X
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists a,b\in X\;\bigl(a<b\land \forall c\in A\;(c\le a\lor b\le c)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }X\text{ be a linearly ordered set and }A\subseteq X.\\
&A\text{ is not order dense in }X
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists a,b\in X\;\bigl(a<b\land \forall c\in A\;(c\le a\lor b\le c)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_predicate:
\[
\neg\operatorname{OrderDenseSubset}(A,X)\Longleftrightarrow
\exists a,b\in X\;\bigl(a<b\land \forall c\in A\;(c\le a\lor b\le c)\bigr).
\]
nodes.failure_modes: Order density fails when there is a nonempty open interval of $X$ that contains no point of $A$.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\neg\operatorname{OrderDenseSubset}(A,X)
=
\underbrace{\exists a,b\in X\;(a<b)}_{\text{nonempty interval}}
\;\land\;
\underbrace{\forall c\in A\;(c\le a\lor b\le c)}_{\text{no point of }A\text{ lies between }a\text{ and }b}.
\]
nodes.source_text: Order density is an interval-penetration property. It ignores metric distance and asks only whether every ordered gap contains a point of the subset. A subset can therefore be order dense in $X$ precisely when no nonempty open interval of $X$ is missed entirely by that subset.

nodes.question: State the theorem: Density of the Rational Numbers in $ $.
nodes.statement_display: For every $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ with $a<b$, there exists $q\in\mathbb{Q}$ such that $a<q<b$.
nodes.statement_tex: For every $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ with $a<b$, there exists $q\in\mathbb{Q}$ such that $a<q<b$.

\]

\[

\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\exists a,b\in\mathbb{R}\;\bigl(a<b\land \forall q\in\mathbb{Q}\;(q\le a\lor b\le q)\bigr).
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\exists a,b\in\mathbb{R}\;\bigl(a<b\land \forall q\in\mathbb{Q}\;(q\le a\lor b\le q)\bigr).
\]
nodes.failure_modes: The theorem would fail precisely if some nonempty real interval contained no rational number.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\neg\operatorname{OrderDenseSubset}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R})
=
\underbrace{\exists a,b\in\mathbb{R}\;(a<b)}_{\text{nonempty real interval}}
\;\land\;
\underbrace{\forall q\in\mathbb{Q}\;(q\le a\lor b\le q)}_{\text{no rational lies inside}}.
\]
nodes.source_text: Rational numbers penetrate every real interval. The theorem does not say that every real number is rational; it says that rational numbers are never separated from a real interval by a positive order gap. This is the interval form of rational density in the real line.

nodes.name: Bound
nodes.question: State the definition: Bound.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\le)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$, and let $b\in S$. The element $b$ is a \emph{bound} for $A$ if and only if $b$ is a uniform one-sided comparison point for all elements of $A$:
\[
\operatorname{Bound}(b,A)
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl[\forall x\in A\;(x\le b)\bigr]
\lor
\bigl[\forall x\in A\;(b\le x)\bigr].
\]

nodes.question: State the definition: Minimum.
nodes.statement_display: Let $(S,\le)$ be an ordered set, $A\subseteq S$, and $m\in S$. The element $m$ is the \emph{minimum} of $A$ if and only if $m\in A$ and $m$ is a lower bound of $A$.

\begin{aligned}

\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(m\in A \land \forall x\in A\;(m\le x)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:

\]

\begin{aligned}

\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(m\notin A \lor \exists x\in A\;(m\nleq x)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}

nodes.failure_modes: Failure occurs either because $m$ is not a member of $A$, or because some element of $A$ lies strictly below $m$, violating the global lower-bound condition.
nodes.source_text: A minimum point both belongs to the set and sits at its absolute bottom: every other element rests above it in the ambient order. The definition splits into the membership requirement, ensuring the bound is realized, and the universal inequality that promotes the element from a mere lower bound to a genuine extremal. Failure arises if the candidate lies outside the set or if another element dips below it; geometrically, the set either has no realized floor at that point or its supposed floor is undercut elsewhere.

nodes.failure_modes: The property fails either because the candidate value is missing from $A$ or because some element of $A$ sits strictly above it, violating the domination requirement.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\neg \operatorname{Maximum}(M,A)
=
\underbrace{(M \notin A)}_{\text{membership failure}}
\;\lor\;
\underbrace{\bigl(\exists x \in A\;(M < x)\bigr)}_{\text{domination failure}}.
\]
nodes.source_text: A maximum is an element of the set that simultaneously belongs to the set and dominates it under the ambient order. The domination clause guarantees that no point of $A$ lies above the maximum, so the element captures the extreme right edge of the subset. Failure occurs either when the supposed extremal is not actually part of the set or when another member protrudes farther to the right, showing the candidate was not truly maximal. In geometric terms, the maximum is the endpoint where the subset comes to rest when viewed along the ordering axis.

nodes.name: Supremum
nodes.question: State the definition: Supremum.
nodes.statement_display: Let $(S,\le)$ be an ordered set, let $A \subseteq S$, and let $s \in S$. The element $s$ is the supremum of $A$ if and only if $s$ is an upper bound of $A$ and every upper bound $u$ of $A$ satisfies $s \le u$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $(S,\le)$ be an ordered set, let $A \subseteq S$, and let $s \in S$. The element $s$ is the supremum of $A$ if and only if $s$ is an upper bound of $A$ and every upper bound $u$ of $A$ satisfies $s \le u$.
nodes.negation_predicate:
\[
\neg\operatorname{Supremum}(s,A) \Longleftrightarrow \bigl(\exists x \in A\, (s < x)\bigr) \lor \bigl(\exists u \in S\,(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A) \land u < s)\bigr).
\]
nodes.failure_modes: The definition fails in exactly two ways: either $s$ is not an upper bound of $A$, or there exists a strictly smaller upper bound $u$ of $A$, showing that $s$ is not the least among all upper bounds.
nodes.source_text: The supremum of $A$ is the smallest ambient element that dominates the whole set. It exists precisely when $s$ bounds $A$ from above and no stricter bound sits below it. Failure occurs either because $A$ pokes above $s$ or because another upper bound nestles strictly beneath $s$, contradicting minimality. Geometrically, the supremum is the leftmost point in the order that caps the set, so every other cap must lie to its right.

nodes.statement_display: Let $S$ be an ordered set with the least upper bound property. If $A\subseteq S$ is nonempty and bounded above in $S$, then $A$ has a supremum in $S$.

\bigl[

\Longrightarrow

\]

nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Assume that $S$ has the Least Upper Bound Property. Let $A \subseteq S$ be nonempty and bounded above in $S$. By the Least Upper Bound Property, there exists an element $s \in S$ that is a least upper bound of $A$ in $S$. By definition, this means that $s$ is a supremum of $A$ in $S$. Hence
\[
\exists s \in S \; \operatorname{Supremum}(s,A).
\]
Therefore every nonempty subset of $S$ that is bounded above in $S$ has a supremum in $S$.

nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let $m_1, m_2 \in A$ be maxima of $A$. By the definition of maximum, $m_1$ is an upper bound of $A$; since $m_2 \in A$, it follows that $m_2 \le m_1$. Similarly, $m_2$ is an upper bound of $A$; since $m_1 \in A$, it follows that $m_1 \le m_2$. By the antisymmetry of the $\le$ relation on $\mathbb{R}$, $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \le m_1$ imply $m_1 = m_2$.
nodes.proof_idea: This is a uniqueness proof by antisymmetry. It assumes two candidates for the maximum and uses the double-inclusion logic of upper bounds to force their equality.
nodes.source_text: A maximum is not merely a high point of the set; it is the greatest point of the set. If two elements both claim that role, each must sit above the other, and antisymmetry of the real order forces them to be the same number.

nodes.question: State the proposition: Supremum in the Set Is the Maximum.
nodes.statement_display: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and let $s=\sup A$. If $s\in A$, then $s$ is a maximum of $A$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and let $s=\sup A$. If $s\in A$, then $s$ is a maximum of $A$.
nodes.formal:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\text{ and }s\in\mathbb{R}.\\
&\bigl[s=\sup A\;\land\;s\in A\bigr]
\Longrightarrow
s\text{ is a maximum of }A.
\end{aligned}
\]

\end{aligned}
\]

&s=\sup A,\quad s\in A,\quad\text{and }s\text{ is not a maximum of }A
\end{aligned}
\]
is impossible.

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\text{ and }s\in\mathbb{R}.\\
&s=\sup A,\quad s\in A,\quad\text{and }s\text{ is not a maximum of }A
\end{aligned}
\]

\[

\]

nodes.failure_modes: The implication could fail only if the least upper bound belonged to the set but did not dominate every element of the set. That cannot happen because every supremum is already an upper bound.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Supremum}(s,A)\land s\in A
&\Longrightarrow
\underbrace{\forall x\in A\;(x\le s)}_{s\text{ is an upper bound}}\\
&\qquad\land
\underbrace{s\in A}_{s\text{ belongs to the set}}
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{Maximum}(s,A).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a non-empty set bounded above, and let $s = \sup A$. By the definition of the supremum, $s$ is an upper bound of $A$, which implies $s \ge a$ for all $a \in A$. 

The definition of a maximum $m$ of a set $A$ requires two conditions:
1. $m \in A$
2. $m \ge a$ for all $a \in A$

We are given the hypothesis that $s \in A$, satisfying the first condition. From the definition of supremum, we have $s \ge a$ for all $a \in A$, satisfying the second condition. Therefore, $s$ satisfies the definition of the maximum of $A$. Since the maximum is unique, we conclude that $s = \max A$.

nodes.question: State the lemma: Subset Inclusion Preserves Upper Bounds.
nodes.statement_display: Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $u$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $u$ is an upper bound of $A$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $u$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $u$ is an upper bound of $A$.

\end{aligned}
\]

\]

\Longleftrightarrow

\end{aligned}

nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ such that $A \subseteq B$. Let $u \in \mathbb{R}$ be an upper bound of $B$. By the definition of an upper bound, $b \le u$ for all $b \in B$. Since $A \subseteq B$, every element $a \in A$ is also an element of $B$. It follows that $a \le u$ for all $a \in A$. Thus, $u$ is an upper bound of $A$.

\end{aligned}
\]

\end{aligned}

nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let $s_B = \sup B$. Then $s_B$ is an upper bound of $B$, so
\[
\forall b \in B,\quad b \le s_B.
\]
Since $A \subseteq B$, it follows that
\[
\forall a \in A,\quad a \le s_B,
\]
so $s_B$ is an upper bound of $A$. Let $s_A = \sup A$. Since $s_A$ is the least upper bound of $A$, and $s_B$ is an upper bound of $A$, it follows that
\[
s_A \le s_B.
\]
nodes.proof_idea: Direct argument using the definition of upper bound and the minimality property of the supremum.
nodes.source_text: Making a set larger can only push its least ceiling upward or leave it unchanged. It cannot lower the supremum, because the larger set contains all of the old points that already had to be bounded.

nodes.question: State the proposition: Upper Bound Comparison with the Supremum.
nodes.statement_display: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let $s=\sup A$. For $u\in\mathbb{R}$, the number $u$ is an upper bound of $A$ if and only if $s\le u$.

\]
is impossible when $s=\sup A$.

\exists u\in\mathbb{R}\;

nodes.failure_modes: There are two apparent ways the equivalence could fail. Either an upper bound lies below the supremum, contradicting leastness, or a number above the supremum fails to bound the set, contradicting that the supremum already bounds the set.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
$(\Rightarrow)$ Suppose $u$ is an upper bound of $A$. Since $s = \sup A$, $s$ is the least upper bound of $A$, so $s \le u$.

$(\Leftarrow)$ Suppose $s \le u$. Since $s$ is an upper bound of $A$, we have $a \le s$ for all $a \in A$. By transitivity of $\le$ on $\mathbb{R}$, $a \le u$ for all $a \in A$. Hence $u$ is an upper bound of $A$.
nodes.proof_idea: Equivalence proof: each direction follows directly from the definition of supremum and the transitivity of the order on $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.source_text: Once the supremum is known, all upper bounds are exactly the real numbers at or above it. The supremum is therefore the threshold where upper bounds begin.

nodes.name: Infimum Is Less Than or Equal to the Supremum
nodes.question: State the theorem: Infimum Is Less Than or Equal to the Supremum.
nodes.statement_display: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty, bounded below, and bounded above. Then $\inf A\le \sup A$.
nodes.statement_tex: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty, bounded below, and bounded above. Then $\inf A\le \sup A$.

nodes.failure_modes: The inequality could fail only if the greatest lower bound were strictly above the least upper bound. Any element of the nonempty set must lie between those two bounding values, which rules out this order.
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let $A$ be a non-empty bounded set in $\mathbb{R}$. By the completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, $i = \inf A$ and $s = \sup A$ exist. Since $A \neq \varnothing$, choose $a \in A$. By the definition of infimum, $i \le a$. By the definition of supremum, $a \le s$. By the transitivity of $\le$, $i \le a \le s$, which implies $i \le s$.
nodes.proof_idea: This is a direct proof utilizing a single element of the set as a logical pivot between the lower bound property of the infimum and the upper bound property of the supremum.
nodes.source_text: A nonempty bounded set cannot have its floor above its ceiling. Any point of the set witnesses the bridge from the infimum up to the supremum.

nodes.name: Translation Invariance of the Supremum
nodes.question: State the theorem: Translation Invariance of the Supremum.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Then
\[
 \sup(A+c)=\sup A+c,
 \qquad
 A+c=\{a+c:a\in A\}.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Then
\[
 \sup(A+c)=\sup A+c,
 \qquad
 A+c=\{a+c:a\in A\}.
\]
nodes.negation_display:
\[
\sup(A+c)\ne \sup A+c
\]
is impossible under the stated hypotheses.
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\sup(A+c)\ne \sup A+c
\]
is impossible under the stated hypotheses.
nodes.failure_modes: The formula could fail only if translation either failed to preserve upper bounds or failed to preserve leastness. Adding the same real number to every comparison preserves the order, so neither failure mode can occur.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\forall a\in A\;(a\le s)
&\Longleftrightarrow
\forall a\in A\;(a+c\le s+c),\\
\forall u\,[\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A)\Longrightarrow s\le u]
&\Longleftrightarrow
\forall v\,[\operatorname{UpperBound}(v,A+c)\Longrightarrow s+c\le v].
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.name: Negation Exchanges Supremum and Infimum
nodes.question: State the theorem: Negation Exchanges Supremum and Infimum.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then $-A=\{-a:a\in A\}$ is bounded above and
\[
 \sup(-A)=-\inf A.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:

\[

\]

\]

\]

nodes.failure_modes: The theorem could fail only if negation did not convert lower bounds into upper bounds or did not preserve the extremal threshold after reversing order. The map $x\mapsto -x$ reverses all inequalities, so the exchange is exact.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\forall a\in A\;(t\le a)
&\Longleftrightarrow
\forall a\in A\;(-a\le -t),\\
\operatorname{LowerBound}(v,A)
&\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{UpperBound}(-v,-A).
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let $i = \inf A$. By definition, $i \le a$ for all $a \in A$. Multiplying by $-1$ reverses the inequality, giving $-i \ge -a$ for all $-a \in -A$. Thus, $-i$ is an upper bound of $-A$. To show it is the least upper bound, let $u$ be any upper bound of $-A$. Then $u \ge -a$ for all $a \in A$, which implies $-u \le a$. Thus, $-u$ is a lower bound of $A$. Since $i$ is the greatest lower bound, $i \ge -u$, which implies $-i \le u$. Hence $\sup(-A) = -i = -\inf A$.
nodes.proof_idea: The proof follows a direct argument by showing $- \inf A$ satisfies both conditions of the supremum for set $-A$: it is an upper bound, and it is less than or equal to any other upper bound.
nodes.source_text: Negation reflects the real line through the origin. Floors become ceilings, so the infimum of the original set becomes the negative of the supremum of the reflected set.

nodes.question: State the theorem: Supremum of a Sum Set.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above. Then
\[
 \sup(A+B)=\sup A+\sup B,
 \qquad
 A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above. Then
\[
 \sup(A+B)=\sup A+\sup B,
 \qquad
 A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}.
\]

\[
\sup(A+B)\ne \sup A+\sup B
\]
is impossible under the stated hypotheses.
nodes.negation_formal:
\[
\sup(A+B)\ne \sup A+\sup B
\]
is impossible under the stated hypotheses.
nodes.failure_modes: The equality could fail only if the sum of the two suprema did not bound the sum set, or if it were not the least such bound. The first part follows from adding the two upper-bound inequalities; the second follows by approximating each supremum from within its set.
nodes.failure_mode_decomposition:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a\le \sup A,\quad b\le \sup B
&\Longrightarrow a+b\le \sup A+\sup B,\\
\varepsilon>0
&\Longrightarrow
\exists a\in A,\ b\in B:
\sup A+\sup B-\varepsilon<a+b.
\end{aligned}
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Let $s_a = \sup A$ and $s_b = \sup B$. For any $x \in A+B$, $x = a+b$ for some $a \in A, b \in B$. Since $a \le s_a$ and $b \le s_b$, we have $a+b \le s_a + s_b$, so $s_a + s_b$ is an upper bound of $A+B$. Thus $\sup(A+B) \le s_a + s_b$. Conversely, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist $a \in A$ and $b \in B$ such that $a > s_a - \varepsilon/2$ and $b > s_b - \varepsilon/2$. Then $a+b > s_a + s_b - \varepsilon$. Since $a+b \in A+B$, this shows $\sup(A+B) \ge s_a + s_b$. Therefore, $\sup(A+B) = s_a + s_b$.
nodes.proof_idea: The proof utilizes a double-inequality strategy: first proving $\sup(A+B) \le \sup A + \sup B$ via the upper bound property, and then $\sup(A+B) \ge \sup A + \sup B$ via the $\varepsilon$-characterization of the supremum.
nodes.source_text: The highest limiting value of all pairwise sums is obtained by combining values that approach the separate ceilings of $A$ and $B$.

nodes.statement_display: Let $(S,\le_S)$ and $(T,\le_T)$ be ordered sets, and let $A\subseteq S\cap T$. Whether $u$ is an upper bound of $A$ must be interpreted relative to the chosen ambient order.

nodes.question: State the definition: Relative Neighborhood.
nodes.statement_display: Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $a \in E$. A set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a neighborhood of $a$ in $E$ if and only if there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $U = E \cap (a-\delta, a+\delta)$. Equivalently, every neighborhood of $a$ in $E$ is a set of the form $U_E(a) := E \cap (a-\delta, a+\delta)$ for some $\delta > 0$.

nodes.name: Continuity at a Point
nodes.question: State the definition: Continuity at a Point.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $c \in A$. The function $f$ is \textbf{continuous at $c$} if and only if
\[
\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists \delta > 0 \;\forall x \in A :
\bigl(|x-c| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-f(c)| < \varepsilon\bigr).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
