nodes.name: Self Additive Inverse
nodes.question: State the lemma: Self Additive Inverse.
nodes.statement_display:
In any Boolean ring $R$,
\[
p + p = 0 \qquad \text{for all } p \in R.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
In any Boolean ring $R$,
\[
p + p = 0 \qquad \text{for all } p \in R.
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\forall p \in R{:}\; p + p = 0.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\forall p \in R{:}\; p + p = 0.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
Apply idempotence to the element $p + p$:
\[
(p + p) \cdot (p + p) = p + p. \tag{i}
\]
Expand the left side using right distributivity~(9), then left
distributivity~(8), then collapse each $p \cdot p = p$ by
idempotence~(11):
\[
(p + p) \cdot (p + p)
  \;\overset{(9)}{=}\; p\cdot(p+p) + p\cdot(p+p)
  \;\overset{(8)}{=}\; (p^2 + p^2) + (p^2 + p^2)
  \;\overset{p^2=p}{=}\; (p + p) + (p + p). \tag{ii}
\]
Combining (i) and (ii): $(p+p) + (p+p) = p+p$.
Setting $s = p+p$, the equation $s + s = s$ gives $s = 0$
by adding $-s$ and applying associativity, the inverse law,
and the identity law.
Hence $p + p = 0$.
nodes.proof_idea:
The proof is direct.
The strategy applies idempotence twice: once to $p + p$ as a
whole (Step~1) and once to $p$ individually (Step~4), with
distributivity (Steps~2--3) connecting the two applications.
The conclusion follows by a standard additive cancellation
(Step~6) using only the group axioms for $(R,+)$.
No circularity arises: the proof never assumes $1 + 1 = 0$
or any consequence of characteristic~$2$.
Both $p + p = 0$ and $1 + 1 = 0$ are consequences of
idempotence; this proof derives the former directly without
appealing to the latter.
The Lean~4 formalisation is \texttt{AdditiveIdempotence} in
\texttt{LRA/VolumeI/BooleanAlgebra/BooleanAlgebraDefinitions.lean}.
nodes.source_text:
This is Halmos consequence~(a): idempotence of multiplication
forces the additive structure to have characteristic~2.  The proof
expands $(p+q)^2$ by distributivity and idempotence, cancels $p$
and $q$, then sets $p = q$ to obtain $p + p = 0$.  The Lean~4
formalisation is \texttt{AdditiveIdempotence} in
\texttt{BooleanAlgebraDefinitions.lean}.

nodes.name: Self Negation
nodes.question: State the lemma: Self Negation.
nodes.statement_display:
In any Boolean ring $R$,
\[
-p = p \qquad \text{for all } p \in R.
\]
nodes.statement_tex:
In any Boolean ring $R$,
\[
-p = p \qquad \text{for all } p \in R.
\]
nodes.formal:
\[
\forall p \in R{:}\; -p = p.
\]
nodes.fully_quantified_form:
\[
\forall p \in R{:}\; -p = p.
\]
nodes.proof_sketch:
\LRAProofBodyStart
By \hyperref[lem:self-additive-inverse]{Self Additive Inverse}, $p + p = 0$.
By the additive inverse axiom~(7), $p + (-p) = 0$.
Since both $p$ and $-p$ satisfy the equation $p + x = 0$, and additive
inverses are unique in any group (a standard group theory fact applied to
the abelian group $(R,+)$), we conclude $-p = p$.
nodes.proof_idea:
A one-step uniqueness argument. Self Additive Inverse shows $p$ is its
own additive inverse; the ring axiom asserts $-p$ is also an additive
inverse of $p$; uniqueness of inverses in the underlying group forces
$p = -p$. The proof has no calculation content --- it is purely structural.
nodes.source_text:
This follows immediately from \ref{lem:self-additive-inverse}.
Since $p + p = 0$ and $p + (-p) = 0$ both hold, the uniqueness of
additive inverses gives $-p = p$.  The negation operation is
therefore the identity map on any Boolean ring.  Halmos uses this

nodes.name: Lambda Terms
nodes.question: State the definition: Lambda Terms.
nodes.statement_display:
The set $\Lambda$ of $\lambda$-terms is defined inductively as follows:

- Every variable $x$ is a $\lambda$-term.
- If $M$ is a $\lambda$-term and $x$ is a variable, then
 \[
 \lambda x.\,M
 \]
 is a $\lambda$-term.
- If $M$ and $N$ are $\lambda$-terms, then
 \[
 MN
 \]
 is a $\lambda$-term.

nodes.source_text:
The $\lambda$-terms are the smallest set closed under three constructions:
variables, abstraction (function formation), and application (function
evaluation). This inductive definition plays the same role as recursive
definitions in analysis or algebra: every $\lambda$-term is built from
variables by finitely many applications of abstraction and application.

nodes.name: First-Order Language $ $
nodes.question: State the definition: First-Order Language $ $.
nodes.statement_display:
A \textbf{first-order language} $\mathcal{L}$ consists of three (possibly
empty) sets of non-logical symbols:
- a set $\mathcal{R}$ of \textbf{relation symbols} (also called
 \emph{predicate symbols}), each assigned a fixed arity $n \geq 1$;
- a set $\mathcal{F}$ of \textbf{function symbols}, each assigned a
 fixed \textbf{arity} $n \geq 0$ (0-ary function symbols are
 \emph{constant symbols});
- a set $\mathcal{C}$ of \textbf{constant symbols} (equivalently,
 0-ary function symbols --- listed separately for emphasis).
Together with the logical symbols common to all first-order languages
(variables, connectives $\lnot, \land, \lor, \to, \leftrightarrow$,
quantifiers $\forall, \exists$, equality $=$, parentheses), the triple
$(\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{R}, \mathcal{C})$ determines $\mathcal{L}$.

nodes.name: $ $-Structure
nodes.question: State the definition: $ $-Structure.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\mathcal{L} = (\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{R}, \mathcal{C})$ be a
first-order language.
An \textbf{$\mathcal{L}$-structure} $\mathcal{M}$ consists of:
- a non-empty set $M$ called the \textbf{domain} (or
 \textbf{universe}) of $\mathcal{M}$, written $|\mathcal{M}|$;
- for each $n$-ary relation symbol $R \in \mathcal{R}$,
 a relation $R^{\mathcal{M}} \subseteq M^n$;
- for each $n$-ary function symbol $f \in \mathcal{F}$,
 a function $f^{\mathcal{M}} : M^n \to M$;
- for each constant symbol $c \in \mathcal{C}$,
 a distinguished element $c^{\mathcal{M}} \in M$.
The superscript notation $f^{\mathcal{M}}, R^{\mathcal{M}}, c^{\mathcal{M}}$
denotes the \textbf{interpretation} of each symbol in $\mathcal{M}$.

nodes.name: Variable Assignment
nodes.question: State the definition: Variable Assignment.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $\mathcal{L}$-structure with domain $M$, and let
$\mathrm{Var} = \{v_1, v_2, v_3, \ldots\}$ be a fixed countable set of
first-order variables.

A \textbf{variable assignment} (or \textbf{environment}) for $\mathcal{M}$
is a function $s : \mathrm{Var} \to M$.

For a variable assignment $s$, a variable $v_i$, and an element $a \in M$,
write $s[v_i \mapsto a]$ for the assignment that agrees with $s$ on all
variables except $v_i$, where it returns $a$:
\[
 s[v_i \mapsto a](v_j) =
 \begin{cases}
 a & \text{if } j = i, \\
 s(v_j) & \text{if } j \neq i.
 \end{cases}
\]

nodes.name: Term Evaluation
nodes.question: State the definition: Term Evaluation.
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $\mathcal{L}$-structure and $s : \mathrm{Var} \to M$
a variable assignment.
The \textbf{evaluation} $s(t) \in M$ of an $\mathcal{L}$-term $t$ under
$s$ is defined inductively:
- If $t = v_i$ is a variable, then $s(t) = s(v_i)$.
- If $t = c$ is a constant symbol, then $s(t) = c^{\mathcal{M}}$.
- If $t = f(t_1, \ldots, t_n)$ for an $n$-ary function symbol $f$,
 then $s(t) = f^{\mathcal{M}}(s(t_1), \ldots, s(t_n))$.
